question.question: Is SOP-FIN-005 (Know Your Customer Verification) compliant with SOC 2 vendor management, data classification, and processing integrity criteria?
question.expected_answer: Gap. The SOP lacks a vendor / third-party risk assessment process (CC9.2), has no documented system availability or processing integrity commitments (A1, PI1 if those categories are in scope), and is missing a data classification scheme linked to confidentiality controls (CC6.1, C1). For a KYC SOP that depends heavily on third-party data providers, the vendor gap is particularly material.

output.answer:
Based on the SOP text, **SOP-FIN-005 is partially compliant** with the relevant SOC 2 criteria. It is strongest on **processing integrity**, partially addresses **data classification/confidentiality**, and has material gaps for **vendor management**.

| Area | SOC 2 criteria | Assessment | Rationale |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Vendor management | **CC9.2**; related risk assessment under **CC3.2** | **Partial / gap** | SOC 2 requires the entity to establish vendor engagement requirements covering scope, roles, compliance requirements, and service levels; evaluate vendor-related vulnerabilities; inventory, tier, and periodically assess vendor/business partner risks; and assign accountability for vendor risk management (**SOC 2 CC9.2**). SOP-FIN-005 identifies several KYC vendors and processors—Onfido, LexisNexis, Thomson Reuters CLEAR, World-Check One, AWS, Splunk, Equinix—and assigns “Third-Party KYC Data Processor Oversight” in the RACI matrix (**SOP-FIN-005 §§3.1, 5.1, 5.7, 6.2–6.5**). However, the SOP does **not** define a vendor inventory, tiering methodology, periodic vendor risk reviews, vendor due diligence evidence, SLA monitoring, SOC report review, subservice-organization controls, or ongoing vendor performance/risk monitoring. It also states general vendor procurement due diligence is out of scope and governed by SOP-PROC-004 (**SOP-FIN-005 §1.2**), so this SOP alone does not satisfy SOC 2 vendor management expectations. |
| Data classification and confidentiality | **CC2.1**, **CC6.1**, **C1.1**, **C1.2** | **Partial** | SOC 2 expects information to be classified by relevant characteristics such as PII, confidential customer information, and intellectual property to support control design (**SOC 2 CC2.1**). SOC 2 also expects information assets to be inventoried, classified, and managed, with access restricted using classification and related rules (**SOC 2 CC6.1**). Confidentiality criteria require confidential information to be defined, identified, retained no longer than necessary, protected during retention, and destroyed at the end of retention (**SOC 2 C1.1, C1.2**). SOP-FIN-005 identifies KYC personal data fields, biometric data, beneficial ownership data, EDD financial records, SAR/STR documentation, and DSRR logs; applies RBAC, MFA, encryption, logging, retention, and secure purge controls (**SOP-FIN-005 §§5.1–5.9, 6.1–6.3**). The gap is that it does not expressly assign formal data classification labels or a classification matrix to KYC data categories—for example, “Restricted,” “Confidential,” “PII,” “biometric/special category,” “financial crime sensitive,” or “regulatory records”—nor does it map each class to handling, sharing, masking, export, and retention rules. |
| Processing integrity | **PI1.1–PI1.5** | **Mostly compliant, with minor gaps** | SOC 2 processing integrity concerns whether processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized (**SOC 2, Trust Services Categories description, Processing Integrity**). PI1.1 requires defined processing objectives, data definitions, and product/service specifications; PI1.2 requires controls over complete and accurate inputs; PI1.3 requires policies and procedures over system processing; PI1.4 requires outputs to be complete, accurate, timely, and made available to intended parties; and PI1.5 requires complete, accurate, timely storage of inputs, in-process items, and outputs (**SOC 2 PI1.1–PI1.5**). SOP-FIN-005 defines KYC workflows, required data fields, acceptable documents, verification thresholds, manual review steps, watchlist screening, risk scoring, EDD triggers, SLAs, audit logging, retention, and KPIs (**SOP-FIN-005 §§5.1–5.7, 6.3, 7.1–7.3**). These controls substantially support input validity, completeness, accuracy, timeliness, and authorization. Remaining gaps are that the SOP relies on SOP-FIN-006 for the detailed risk scoring validation methodology (**SOP-FIN-005 §10.1**) and does not fully specify reconciliation/quality assurance controls over automated outputs, vendor-returned IDV results, or completeness/accuracy validation of downstream KYC reports and customer-facing outputs. |

**Required remediation to reach full compliance:**

1. **Add a KYC vendor management section** mapping to SOC 2 **CC9.2**, including vendor inventory, criticality tiering, due diligence, security/privacy review, SLA requirements, SOC report review, issue remediation, periodic reassessment, and subservice-organization/control reliance.
2. **Add a KYC data classification matrix** mapping each KYC data type to classification, permitted users, storage location, encryption/masking/export rules, retention period, and destruction method, aligned to **CC2.1, CC6.1, C1.1, and C1.2**.
3. **Strengthen processing integrity evidence requirements** by adding QA/reconciliation steps for IDV vendor responses, risk score outputs, sanctions screening results, adverse decision notices, and periodic KYC reporting, aligned to **PI1.1–PI1.5**.

Compliance level: partial

question.question: Is SOP-HR-001 (Employee Onboarding and Access Provisioning) compliant with HIPAA on de-identification, breach notification, and minimum-necessary access?
question.expected_answer: Gap. SOP-HR-001 has no PHI de-identification methodology (neither Safe Harbor §164.514(b)(2) nor Expert Determination §164.514(b)(1)), is missing breach-notification procedures entirely (no reference to §164.400-414), and lacks documented minimum-necessary policies for PHI access (§164.502(b)). These are foundational HIPAA controls; absence is a material gap.

output.answer:
SOP-HR-001 is **partially compliant** with HIPAA for the requested topics. It is strong on **minimum-necessary / least-privilege access provisioning**, but it has clear gaps for **de-identification** and **breach notification**.

| HIPAA topic | Assessment | Rationale |
|---|---:|---|
| De-identification | **Gap** | HIPAA requires de-identification either by expert determination or removal of specified identifiers with no actual knowledge of re-identification risk. SOP-HR-001 does not define or reference either method. |
| Breach notification | **Gap** | HIPAA requires procedures for notifying affected individuals, HHS, media in certain cases, and covered entities by business associates. SOP-HR-001 does not contain a breach-notification workflow, timelines, content requirements, or reporting responsibilities. |
| Minimum-necessary access | **Mostly compliant / minor gaps** | SOP-HR-001 implements least privilege, RBAC/ABAC, PHI approval attributes, training prerequisites, manager verification, and access reviews. However, it should more explicitly map workforce classes to PHI categories and conditions of access as HIPAA requires. |

## 1. De-identification — Gap

HIPAA permits information to be treated as de-identified only if it meets the de-identification standard in **45 CFR § 164.514(a)** and one of the implementation methods in **45 CFR § 164.514(b)**: either an expert determines and documents that re-identification risk is very small, or the organization removes the listed identifiers and has no actual knowledge that the remaining information can identify the individual. HIPAA also treats properly de-identified information as outside the Privacy Rule, subject to the re-identification-code restrictions in **45 CFR § 164.502(d)** and **§ 164.514(c)**.

SOP-HR-001 does mention PHI/ePHI and controls access to PHI-bearing environments, especially Snowflake and Clinical AI/MedInsight data platforms. However, it does **not** define:

- the HIPAA **expert determination** process;
- the HIPAA **safe harbor** removal of identifiers;
- documentation of de-identification methods and results;
- rules for re-identification codes;
- who may create, approve, or validate de-identified datasets.

Because the SOP governs access to PHI-bearing databases but does not describe or reference HIPAA-compliant de-identification controls, it is **not compliant for de-identification** under **45 CFR § 164.514(a)–(c)** and **§ 164.502(d)**.

## 2. Breach notification — Gap

HIPAA requires a covered entity, after discovery of a breach of unsecured PHI, to notify each affected individual without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after discovery. The notice must include what happened, types of PHI involved, protective steps, mitigation/investigation actions, and contact procedures. See **45 CFR § 164.404(a)–(c)**.

HIPAA also requires:

- notice to HHS Secretary, with different timing for breaches involving 500 or more individuals versus fewer than 500 individuals, under **45 CFR § 164.408**;
- media notice for breaches involving more than 500 residents of a state or jurisdiction under **45 CFR § 164.406**;
- business associate notice to the covered entity without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery under **45 CFR § 164.410**;
- documentation/burden of proof that required notifications were made or that the event was not a breach under **45 CFR § 164.414**.

SOP-HR-001 includes some access-error handling, misprovisioned-access metrics, and escalation for provisioning failures, but it does not include a HIPAA breach notification procedure. Specifically, it lacks:

- breach identification and escalation criteria;
- distinction between security incidents and HIPAA breaches;
- 60-day notification deadline;
- affected-individual notice content;
- HHS reporting;
- media notification criteria;
- business associate-to-covered entity notification duties;
- breach log and documentation requirements.

Therefore, SOP-HR-001 is **not compliant for HIPAA breach notification** under **45 CFR §§ 164.404, 164.406, 164.408, 164.410, and 164.414**.

## 3. Minimum-necessary access — Mostly compliant, with minor gaps

HIPAA’s minimum necessary rule requires a covered entity to identify workforce persons or classes of persons who need PHI access, identify the PHI categories and conditions of access needed for each class, and make reasonable efforts to limit access accordingly. See **45 CFR § 164.514(d)(2)**. HIPAA’s Security Rule also requires workforce security and information access management procedures to ensure appropriate ePHI access and prevent inappropriate access, including authorization, clearance, access establishment, review, and modification. See **45 CFR § 164.308(a)(3)** and **§ 164.308(a)(4)**. HIPAA also requires covered entities and business associates to protect against impermissible uses/disclosures and ensure workforce compliance under **45 CFR § 164.306(a)**.

SOP-HR-001 contains several controls that align well with these requirements:

- It states access is based on **least privilege** and role-based provisioning.
- It uses Workday attributes and Okta groups to provision access by job title, department, manager, and business unit.
- It says production data/platform access is **not provisioned by default**.
- It requires separate approval for exceptional or elevated access.
- It requires PHI-bearing Snowflake access to have `data_access_level = "PHI-APPROVED"`.
- It requires HIPAA training and Clinical Data Stewardship training before PHI access.
- It requires CPO/DPO approval for access to ePHI beyond role defaults.
- It requires Day 5 manager verification that sensitive systems are not reachable unless explicitly provisioned.
- It requires T+14 new-hire access attestation and semiannual access reviews.

These controls substantially support HIPAA’s workforce-security and access-management requirements in **45 CFR § 164.308(a)(3)–(4)** and minimum-necessary requirements in **45 CFR § 164.514(d)(2)**.

However, SOP-HR-001 should be strengthened by explicitly documenting:

- the specific workforce classes/personas that need PHI access;
- the specific categories of PHI each class may access;
- the conditions under which access is permitted;
- how the `roles-matrix.yaml` maps to HIPAA minimum-necessary determinations;
- how access requests involving PHI are evaluated against minimum-necessary criteria, not just security risk.

So, for minimum-necessary access, the SOP is **largely compliant but not fully complete** against **45 CFR § 164.514(d)(2)**.

## Required remediation

To make SOP-HR-001 HIPAA-compliant for the three requested areas, Meridian should add or cross-reference:

1. **De-identification procedure**
   - Expert determination workflow.
   - Safe harbor identifier-removal checklist.
   - Documentation and approval requirements.
   - Re-identification-code controls.
   - References to **45 CFR § 164.514(a)–(c)** and **§ 164.502(d)**.

2. **Breach notification procedure**
   - Workforce reporting obligations.
   - Breach-risk assessment and escalation.
   - Individual notice within 60 days.
   - HHS reporting.
   - Media notice criteria.
   - Business associate notification duties.
   - Breach log and evidence retention.
   - References to **45 CFR §§ 164.404, 164.406, 164.408, 164.410, and 164.414**.

3. **Minimum-necessary access mapping**
   - Include or attach the PHI-access role matrix.
   - Map job roles to PHI categories and access conditions.
   - Require approvers to document minimum-necessary justification for PHI access.
   - Reference **45 CFR § 164.514(d)(2)** and **§ 164.308(a)(3)–(4)**.

Compliance level: partial

The notification may be provided in one or more mailings as information is available.

(ii) If the covered entity knows the individual is deceased and has the address of the next of kin or personal representative of the individual (as specified under § 164.502(g)(4) of subpart E), written notification by first-class mail to either the next of kin or personal representative of the individual. The notification may be provided in one or more mailings as information is available.

(i) In the case in which there is insufficient or out-of-date contact information for fewer than 10 individuals, then such substitute notice may be provided by an alternative form of written notice, telephone, or other means.

(ii) In the case in which there is insufficient or out-of-date contact information for 10 or more individuals, then such substitute notice shall:

(A) Be in the form of either a conspicuous posting for a period of 90 days on the home page of the Web site of the covered entity involved, or conspicuous notice in major print or broadcast media in geographic areas where the individuals affected by the breach likely reside; and

(B) Include a toll-free phone number that remains active for at least 90 days where an individual can learn whether the individual's unsecured protected health information may be included in the breach.

(3) Additional notice in urgent situations. In any case deemed by the covered entity to require urgency because of possible imminent misuse of unsecured protected health information, the covered entity may provide information to individuals by telephone or other means, as appropriate, in addition to notice provided under paragraph (d)(1) of this section.

In the event of a use or disclosure in violation of subpart E, the covered entity or business associate, as applicable, shall have the burden of demonstrating that all notifications were made as required by this subpart or that the use or disclosure did not constitute a breach, as defined at § 164.402.

question.question: Is SOP-ISEC-001 (Information Security Policy Framework) compliant with GDPR's lawful-basis, consent, and international transfer obligations?
question.expected_answer: Gap. The SOP enables cross-border data flows without documented Chapter V safeguards, has no documented Article 6 lawful basis for processing activities under its scope, and lacks consent mechanisms (opt-in, withdrawal, records). An information-security policy that is silent on these is non-compliant for any processing involving EU data subjects.

output.answer:
No. **SOP-ISEC-001 is not sufficient, by itself, to demonstrate compliance with GDPR lawful-basis, consent, and international-transfer obligations.** It contains useful security/governance elements, but it does not define the privacy-law controls needed for these GDPR obligations.

| GDPR obligation | GDPR requirement | SOP-ISEC-001 assessment |
|---|---|---|
| **Lawful basis for processing** | A controller must identify a lawful basis for each processing activity, such as consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests. **GDPR Art. 6(1)**. For health data and other special-category data, processing is prohibited unless an **Art. 9(2)** condition applies, such as explicit consent, health-care purposes, public health, or research/statistical purposes with safeguards. **GDPR Art. 9(1)–(2)**. | **Gap.** The SOP references PII, PHI, health/AI data, and EU operations, but it does not require a lawful-basis assessment, does not map processing purposes to **GDPR Art. 6**, and does not identify **GDPR Art. 9** conditions for health data. The SOP’s “need-to-know,” encryption, de-identification, and access controls are security controls, not lawful-basis determinations. |
| **Consent governance** | Where processing relies on consent, the controller must be able to demonstrate consent; the request must be distinguishable, intelligible, accessible, and in clear/plain language; withdrawal must be possible at any time and as easy as giving consent. **GDPR Art. 7(1)–(3)**. Consent must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous. **GDPR Art. 4(11)**. | **Gap.** The SOP does not define when consent is used, how consent is captured, what evidence is retained, how consent is withdrawn, how consent is separated from other terms, or how consent applies to AI/analytics/clinical data use. |
| **Transparency tied to lawful basis and transfers** | Data subjects must be told the purposes and legal basis for processing, recipients/categories of recipients, retention period, rights, and—where applicable—international-transfer information and safeguards. **GDPR Arts. 13(1)–(2), 14(1)–(2)**. If processing is based on consent, the notice must explain the right to withdraw consent. **GDPR Arts. 13(2)(c), 14(2)(d)**. | **Gap.** The SOP does not require privacy notices, notice review, notice content, linkage between processing purposes and legal bases, or data-subject disclosures about international transfers. |
| **International transfers** | Transfers of personal data to a third country or international organization must comply with GDPR Chapter V and must not undermine GDPR protection. **GDPR Art. 44**. Transfers may rely on an adequacy decision. **GDPR Art. 45**. If no adequacy decision applies, transfers require appropriate safeguards and enforceable data-subject rights/effective remedies, such as Standard Contractual Clauses or Binding Corporate Rules. **GDPR Art. 46(1)–(2)**. Derogations are limited and include explicit informed consent after risk notice, contractual necessity, important public interest, legal claims, or other specific cases. **GDPR Art. 49(1)**. | **Partial / gap.** The SOP identifies global offices and cloud regions, including Boston, London, Berlin, Singapore, Toronto, AWS `us-east-1`, AWS `eu-west-1`, and cross-region replication. It also mentions DPAs for some vendors and that General Counsel approves data processing agreements. But it does **not** require a transfer inventory, transfer-impact assessment, SCCs, adequacy-decision verification, UK/EU transfer distinction, onward-transfer controls, or data-subject notice of safeguards. |
| **Processor and vendor transfers** | A processor must process personal data only on documented controller instructions, including instructions for transfers to a third country or international organization. **GDPR Art. 28(3)(a)**. Processors must provide sufficient guarantees and assist with GDPR compliance. **GDPR Art. 28(1), 28(3)**. | **Partial.** The SOP requires some third-party due diligence and DPAs, but it does not specify GDPR Art. 28 processor clauses, controller authorization for subprocessors, documented transfer instructions, or international-transfer safeguards for vendors/subprocessors. |
| **Accountability / demonstrability** | Controllers must implement appropriate technical and organizational measures and be able to demonstrate GDPR compliance; where proportionate, this includes data-protection policies. **GDPR Art. 24(1)–(2)**. Security controls such as encryption, resilience, restoration, and testing support security of processing. **GDPR Art. 32(1)**. | **Partial.** SOP-ISEC-001 has strong information-security measures—encryption, access controls, monitoring, incident response, training, and policy review—which support **GDPR Art. 32** security. However, those controls do not demonstrate lawful basis, valid consent, or compliant transfers under **GDPR Arts. 6, 7, 9, and 44–49**. |

Additional current-transfer note: the European Commission maintains adequacy decisions under **GDPR Art. 45**, and the EDPB notes that exporters remain responsible for checking whether relevant adequacy decisions remain in force. Source: EDPB international transfers guidance, https://www.edpb.europa.eu/sme-data-protection-guide/international-data-transfers_en; European Commission adequacy decisions page, https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/international-dimension-data-protection/adequacy-decisions_en.

## Required remediation

To make SOP-ISEC-001, or a linked GDPR privacy SOP, compliant for these topics, Meridian should add or cross-reference controls requiring:

1. **Processing inventory / RoPA**
   - For each processing activity: purpose, data categories, data subjects, controller/processor role, recipients, retention, lawful basis under **GDPR Art. 6**, and special-category basis under **GDPR Art. 9** where health data is involved.

2. **Lawful-basis assessment procedure**
   - Require approval by the CPO/DPO or Legal before new processing begins.
   - Require legitimate-interest assessments where relying on **GDPR Art. 6(1)(f)**.
   - Require separate **GDPR Art. 9** justification for health, biometric, genetic, or other special-category data.

3. **Consent-management procedure**
   - Define when consent is relied upon.
   - Require consent records sufficient to demonstrate consent under **GDPR Art. 7(1)**.
   - Require consent language that is clear, plain, distinguishable, and accessible under **GDPR Art. 7(2)**.
   - Require withdrawal mechanisms that are as easy as giving consent under **GDPR Art. 7(3)**.
   - Prohibit bundled or unnecessary consent where service performance does not require the processing, consistent with **GDPR Art. 7(4)**.

4. **Privacy notice controls**
   - Require notices to include purposes, legal bases, recipients, retention, rights, DPO contact, consent-withdrawal rights, automated-decision/profiling information where applicable, and international-transfer safeguards. **GDPR Arts. 13–14**.

5. **International-transfer governance**
   - Maintain an EU/UK transfer inventory.
   - Identify each transfer route: adequacy under **GDPR Art. 45**, SCCs/BCRs or other safeguards under **GDPR Art. 46**, or limited derogation under **GDPR Art. 49**.
   - Require transfer-impact assessments and documented supplementary safeguards where needed.
   - Require onward-transfer controls for subprocessors.
   - Require data-subject notice of transfers and safeguards under **GDPR Arts. 13(1)(f), 14(1)(f), and 15(2)**.

6. **Vendor / processor GDPR clauses**
   - Update TPRM and DPA requirements to include **GDPR Art. 28** processor terms, documented instructions for transfers, subprocessor authorization, audit rights, deletion/return obligations, and assistance with data-subject rights and security obligations.

Compliance level: partial

question.question: Does SOP-PENG-001 (Secure Software Development Lifecycle) meet SOC 2's change-management and monitoring criteria?
question.expected_answer: Partial. A change-management process exists but lacks segregation of duties for approvals (CC8.1 expects independence between requester, developer, and approver). Monitoring is mentioned but alert thresholds and escalation paths are not defined (CC7.2/CC7.3). The skeleton aligns but is not operationally enforceable as the criteria require.

output.answer:
SOP-PENG-001 **partially meets** SOC 2 change-management and monitoring criteria. It is strong on SSDLC gates, testing, documentation, and post-deployment technical monitoring, but it has gaps around **segregation of duties**, **formal monitoring/escalation definition**, and **control-monitoring rigor**.

## Assessment against SOC 2 change management — CC8.1

SOC 2 **CC8.1** requires the entity to “authorize, design, develop or acquire, configure, document, test, approve, and implement changes to infrastructure, data, software, and procedures” to meet objectives. CC8.1’s points of focus include lifecycle change management, pre-change authorization, secure design/development, documentation, tracking, configuration, testing before production, approval before implementation, deployment with segregation of responsibilities, emergency changes, and baseline configuration maintenance.  

### What the SOP covers well

- **Lifecycle management:** SOP-PENG-001 defines a full SSDLC from requirements through design, development, testing, release, operations, and decommissioning in Section 5, which aligns with SOC 2 **CC8.1 — Manages Changes Throughout the System Life Cycle**.
- **Authorization and documentation:** Section 5.1 requires Jira Epics, PRDs, regulatory considerations, security requirements, and security impact ratings; Section 5.5 requires a ServiceNow Change Request with Jira IDs, rollback plan, and evidence of SSDLC approvals. This supports SOC 2 **CC8.1 — Authorizes Changes, Documents Changes, and Tracks System Changes**.
- **Secure design and development:** Section 5.2 requires security architecture review, threat modeling, DFDs, and design-review checklists for Moderate/High changes; Section 5.3 requires secure coding standards, branch protection, peer PR review, SAST, SCA, IaC, and secret scanning. This aligns with SOC 2 **CC8.1 — Designs and Develops Changes** and **Tests System Changes**.
- **Pre-production testing:** Section 5.4 requires security QA, abuser-story testing, DAST, and annual or triggered penetration testing, which aligns with SOC 2 **CC8.1 — Tests System Changes**.
- **Approval before deployment:** Section 5.5 requires an approved ServiceNow Change Request before production deployment, supporting SOC 2 **CC8.1 — Approves System Changes**.
- **Rollback and emergency/exception handling:** Section 5.5 requires rollback plans and post-mortems for failed deployments; Section 8 defines exception tiers and approval authorities. This partially supports SOC 2 **CC8.1 — Provides for Changes Necessary in Emergency Situations**.

### Change-management gaps

1. **Segregation of duties is not consistently enforced.**  
   SOC 2 **CC8.1 — Deploys System Changes** expects implementation with consideration of segregation of responsibilities, such as restricting unilateral development/testing/implementation by a single user. SOP-PENG-001 Section 5.3.2 requires PR author and merger separation only for **Tier-1 production services**; for other services it is merely “recommended.” Section 4.3 also states the process “relies on the author’s integrity for proper segregation.” That is a SOC 2 design weakness for non–Tier-1 systems and potentially for Tier-1 if the Engineering Lead who created or sponsored the change also approves it.

2. **Change approval independence is weak.**  
   SOC 2 **CC8.1 — Approves System Changes** requires approval before implementation. SOP-PENG-001 Section 5.5 routes approval to the Engineering Lead, and Section 3 identifies Engineering Leads as responsible for approving change requests. The SOP does not require independent CAB, peer management approval, or separate production-release authority for higher-risk changes other than notification to the Director of Cloud Infrastructure for Tier-1 services.

3. **Emergency change process is incomplete.**  
   SOC 2 **CC8.1 — Provides for Changes Necessary in Emergency Situations** expects a process for authorizing, designing, testing, approving, and implementing urgent changes. SOP-PENG-001 Section 8 defines exceptions, including emergency hotfix bypassing DAST, but it does not fully specify emergency-change workflow details such as retrospective approval timing, minimum testing evidence, emergency deployment logging, or required post-implementation review.

## Assessment against SOC 2 monitoring criteria — CC4.1, CC7.2, and CC7.3

SOC 2 **CC4.1** requires ongoing and/or separate evaluations to determine whether internal controls are present and functioning, including risk-based scope and frequency, objective separate evaluations, and use of control testing, compliance assessments, vulnerability scans, security assessments, penetration testing, and third-party assessments.  

SOC 2 **CC7.2** requires monitoring system components and operations for anomalies indicative of malicious acts, disasters, or errors, and analyzing anomalies to determine whether they represent security events. Its points of focus include detection policies, procedures, tools, logging unusual activity, anomaly analysis, and monitoring detection tools for effective operation.  

SOC 2 **CC7.3** requires evaluating security events to determine whether they could or did result in failure to meet objectives and taking action to prevent or address failures. Its points of focus include communicating and reviewing detected security events, incident-analysis procedures, and periodic evaluation of response procedures.  

### What the SOP covers well

- **Post-deployment monitoring:** Section 5.5 requires smoke testing and 15-minute Datadog monitoring for error-rate, latency, and traffic anomalies after deployment, supporting SOC 2 **CC7.2 — Monitors system components and operations for anomalies**.
- **Continuous vulnerability and configuration monitoring:** Section 5.6 requires Wiz scanning for production containers and infrastructure, Snyk dependency monitoring, and alerting for configuration drift. This supports SOC 2 **CC7.2 — Implements Detection Policies, Procedures, and Tools**.
- **Security-event monitoring:** Section 7.1 states that the SOC monitors Splunk for CI/CD-related security events such as unauthorized admin access and secret leakage alerts. This supports SOC 2 **CC7.2 — Logging of unusual system activities** and **CC7.3 — Communicates and Reviews Detected Security Events**.
- **Metrics and management reporting:** Section 7.2 defines monthly KPIs for SAST findings, CVE MTTR, threat-model coverage, secure-code-review compliance, lead time, and rollback percentage; Section 7.3 requires monthly SSDLC KPI reporting and quarterly executive risk reporting. This supports SOC 2 **CC4.1 — Ongoing Evaluations**.
- **Separate evaluations:** Section 5.4.3 requires annual external penetration testing for Tier-1 applications, and Section 3.2 assigns the Compliance Officer responsibility for periodic SSDLC audits. These partially support SOC 2 **CC4.1 — Separate Evaluations**.

### Monitoring gaps

1. **Alert thresholds and escalation paths are not formally defined in the SOP.**  
   SOC 2 **CC7.2** expects detection policies, procedures, and tools to be defined and implemented, and SOC 2 **CC7.3** expects detected security events to be communicated and reviewed by responsible personnel. SOP-PENG-001 Section 4.3 states that formal alert thresholds and escalation paths are “managed through team-level operational runbooks,” but the SOP itself does not define required thresholds, required runbook contents, ownership, or approval requirements.

2. **Monitoring-tool effectiveness is not explicitly tested.**  
   SOC 2 **CC7.2 — Monitors Detection Tools for Effective Operation** requires processes to monitor and maintain detection-tool effectiveness. SOP-PENG-001 Section 7.1 says dashboards and SIEM monitoring exist, but it does not require periodic testing of alert rules, log ingestion, Datadog/Splunk/Wiz/Snyk connector health, false-negative review, or simulated detection exercises.

3. **Control monitoring lacks a defined audit cadence and methodology.**  
   SOC 2 **CC4.1** expects ongoing and separate evaluations with risk-based scope/frequency and objective feedback. SOP-PENG-001 Section 7 defines monthly KPIs and quarterly reporting, but “periodic audits” by the Compliance Officer in Section 3.2 are not assigned a minimum frequency, sample size, control-test procedure, evidence requirements, or remediation-tracking process.

4. **Security-event evaluation is delegated to other SOPs but not fully specified here.**  
   SOC 2 **CC7.3** requires procedures to evaluate security events and determine whether they represent incidents. SOP-PENG-001 references SOP-ITOP-001 for incident response and requires post-mortems for failed deployments in Section 5.5, but this SOP does not define criteria for when deployment anomalies or CI/CD alerts become security incidents, who performs the triage, or required documentation.

## Bottom line

SOP-PENG-001 is **substantively aligned** with SOC 2 **CC8.1** for SSDLC-based change management and with SOC 2 **CC4.1, CC7.2, and CC7.3** for monitoring activities, but it is not fully compliant as written. To close the gaps, Meridian should:

- Require enforced segregation of duties for all production changes, not only Tier-1 services.
- Require independent approval for high-risk and production changes.
- Define emergency-change procedures, including retrospective review.
- Incorporate minimum alert thresholds, escalation requirements, and runbook standards.
- Add periodic testing of monitoring-tool effectiveness.
- Define SSDLC control-audit cadence, sampling, evidence, and remediation tracking.

Compliance level: partial

Background .01 ASEC has developed a set of criteria (trust services criteria) to be used when evaluating the suitability of the design and operating effectiveness of controls relevant to the security, availability, or processing in- tegrity of information and systems used to provide products or services, or the confidentiality or privacy of information processed by the systems used to provide products or services at an entity, a division, or an operating unit of an entity. In addition, the trust services criteria may be used when evaluating the design and operating effectiveness of controls relevant to the security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality or privacy of a particular type of information processed by one or more of an entity’s sys- tems or one or more systems used to support a particular function within the entity. Yes. As of 11 June 2026, within the past 12 months the European Commission / AI Office has published official guidance and a code of practice package for the EU AI Act’s general-purpose AI (“GPAI”) model obligations.

| Date | Official item | Status / relevance |
|---|---|---|
| 10 July 2025 | **General-Purpose AI Code of Practice** | Published by the Commission/AI Office as a voluntary compliance tool for GPAI providers. The Commission page states that the Code helps providers comply with the AI Act GPAI rules and was later confirmed by the Commission and AI Board as an adequate voluntary tool. Source: European Commission, “The General-Purpose AI Code of Practice,” https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/contents-code-gpai |
| 18 July 2025 | **Guidelines for providers of general-purpose AI models** | Commission guidelines clarifying the scope of GPAI provider obligations, including who is a GPAI provider, whether exemptions apply, and how the obligations entering into application on 2 August 2025 are interpreted. Source: European Commission, “Guidelines for providers of general-purpose AI models,” https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-gpai-providers |
| 24 July 2025 | **Explanatory Notice and Template for the Public Summary of Training Content** | AI Office/Commission template for the public summary of training content required for GPAI models. This directly implements the AI Act requirement that providers make publicly available a sufficiently detailed training-content summary “according to a template provided by the AI Office.” Source: European Commission, https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/explanatory-notice-and-template-public-summary-training-content-general-purpose-ai-models; AI Act, Art. 53(1)(d). |
| 1 August 2025 | **Commission Opinion / AI Board assessment confirming adequacy of the GPAI Code of Practice** | The Commission and AI Board confirmed the Code as an adequate voluntary tool for demonstrating compliance with the AI Act. Source: European Commission, “Commission Opinion on the assessment of the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice,” https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-opinion-assessment-general-purpose-ai-code-practice |

Regulatory context: the GPAI obligations are in **AI Act Chapter V**. Article 53 requires GPAI model providers to prepare technical documentation, provide information to downstream providers, adopt a copyright-compliance policy, and publish a training-content summary using the AI Office template. Article 55 adds obligations for GPAI models with systemic risk, including model evaluation/adversarial testing, systemic-risk assessment and mitigation, serious-incident reporting, and cybersecurity. Article 56 requires the AI Office and AI Board to facilitate codes of practice covering Articles 53 and 55 and permits providers to rely on such codes to demonstrate compliance until harmonised standards exist. AI Act, Arts. 53, 55, 56.

On **implementing acts** specifically: I found official Commission materials confirming the Code’s adequacy, but not a separate EUR-Lex-published Article 56 implementing act laying down common GPAI rules. That is consistent with Article 56(9), which allows the Commission to issue implementing acts with common rules if a code cannot be finalised or is deemed inadequate by 2 August 2025; here, the Commission/AI Board confirmed the Code’s adequacy. AI Act, Art. 56(6), 56(9).

question.question: Has the Federal Reserve, OCC, or FDIC issued any supervisory guidance, public speeches, or enforcement actions in the past 12 months that update or interpret SR 11-7 for AI/ML model risk management?

output.answer:
Yes. In the past 12 months, the Federal Reserve, OCC, and FDIC issued a **joint revised supervisory guidance** that materially updates the SR 11-7 model-risk framework for AI/ML models, but I did **not** find a public enforcement action specifically interpreting SR 11-7 for AI/ML model risk management.

## Key development: April 17, 2026 revised interagency model-risk guidance

The Federal Reserve, OCC, and FDIC issued **“Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management”** on **April 17, 2026**. Public sources identify it as **Federal Reserve SR 26-2**, **OCC Bulletin 2026-13**, and an FDIC-issued revised model-risk guidance.  
Sources: Federal Reserve SR 26-2 PDF: https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/SR2602.pdf; OCC Bulletin 2026-13: https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/bulletins/2026/bulletin-2026-13.html; FDIC press release: https://www.fdic.gov/news/press-releases/2026/agencies-issue-revised-model-risk-guidance

### How it updates/interprets SR 11-7 for AI/ML

The revised guidance states that the agencies are issuing revised model-risk guidance to “clarify model risk management principles” and set out a **risk-based approach** tailored to a bank’s model-risk profile and operational complexity. That is a direct update to the SR 11-7 framework.  
Citation: **Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management, Sections I–II**.

For AI/ML specifically, the revised guidance defines a “model” as a complex quantitative method, system, or approach applying statistical, economic, or financial theories to process inputs into quantitative estimates, while excluding simple arithmetic and deterministic rule-based processes.  
Citation: **Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management, Section II**.

The guidance expressly addresses AI scope: **generative AI and agentic AI are not within scope**, but the principles apply to **traditional statistical and quantitative models and non-generative, non-agentic AI models**. It also says banks’ broader risk-management and governance practices should guide controls for tools outside the guidance.  
Citation: **Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management, Section II, footnote 3**.

Core SR 11-7 concepts remain, including model risk, effective challenge, model development and use, validation/monitoring, and governance/controls. The revised guidance states that sound model-risk management involves “effective challenge” by objective experts with appropriate expertise, independence, standing, and influence.  
Citation: **Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management, Sections III and VI**.

## Agency-specific notes

### Federal Reserve

Yes. The Federal Reserve issued **SR 26-2** on April 17, 2026, which provides the revised interagency supervisory guidance. It is the clearest Federal Reserve action updating SR 11-7 for AI/ML model-risk management.  
Source: https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/SR2602.pdf  
Citation: **Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management, Sections I–II; Section II footnote 3**.

The Federal Reserve also had recent AI-related public speeches, including Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman’s May 1, 2026 speech, **“Artificial Intelligence in the Financial System,”** and May 14, 2026 remarks noting the Fed’s role in understanding and encouraging risk management for AI and other emerging technologies. These speeches are relevant context, but they do not appear to formally revise SR 11-7 beyond the April 17, 2026 guidance.  
Sources: https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/bowman20260501a.htm; https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/bowman20260514a.htm

### OCC

Yes. The OCC issued **OCC Bulletin 2026-13** and a related news release on April 17, 2026. The OCC release states that the updated guidance discusses model development/use, validation/monitoring, governance/controls, and vendor/third-party products; it also notes that generative AI and agentic AI are not within the scope of the guidance.  
Sources: https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/bulletins/2026/bulletin-2026-13.html; https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/news-releases/2026/nr-occ-2026-29.html  
Citation: **Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management, Sections IV–VI; Section II footnote 3**.

I did not find an OCC public enforcement action in the past 12 months that specifically updates or interprets SR 11-7 for AI/ML model-risk management.

### FDIC

Yes. The FDIC participated in the April 17, 2026 revised interagency guidance and stated that it was rescinding prior FDIC model-risk issuances, including **FIL-22-2017** and **FIL-27-2021**, in connection with the revised guidance.  
Source: https://www.fdic.gov/news/press-releases/2026/agencies-issue-revised-model-risk-guidance  
Citation: **Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management, Sections I–II**.

The FDIC also has 2026 public speeches discussing the policy rationale. In **“Oversight of Prudential Regulators,”** the FDIC described the earlier model-risk guidance as overly prescriptive and challenging for new and emerging modeling techniques, and linked that concern to the revised interagency guidance.  
Source: https://www.fdic.gov/news/speeches/2026/oversight-prudential-regulators

In another 2026 speech, **“Innovation At The Speed Of Markets,”** the FDIC discussed taking a fresh look at model-risk guidance to support innovative technology and a more tailored, risk-based approach.  
Source: https://www.fdic.gov/news/speeches/2026/innovation-speed-markets-how-regulators-pace-technology-0

I did not find an FDIC public enforcement action in the past 12 months that specifically updates or interprets SR 11-7 for AI/ML model-risk management.

## Bottom line

**Yes — the agencies have updated SR 11-7 through the April 17, 2026 revised interagency Model Risk Management guidance.** For AI/ML, the most important interpretive point is that the revised framework applies to **non-generative, non-agentic AI models**, while **generative AI and agentic AI are expressly excluded from the guidance’s scope** but still expected to be governed through appropriate risk-management and control practices.  
Citation: **Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management, Section II, footnote 3**.

Use of models within the banking and financial services industries continues to grow in

Model risk can be mitigated through active and appropriate risk management, recognizing that 
the relevance of model risk depends on the nature, scale, and use of the models in relation to the 
associated business risks.  
This guidance highlights sound principles for effective model risk management. As 
reflected in this guidance, model risk management practices vary from banking organization to 
banking organization. Each banking organization ultimately is responsible for adopting model 
risk management practices that are appropriate and effective for managing the specific risks the 
banking organization faces or is likely to face.

banking organization with a different risk profile or that uses a model for a different purpose.

question.question: Looking at SOP-AIML-009 (Algorithmic Bias Detection and Mitigation) against EU AI Act Articles 9, 27, and 49, which specific procedures or artefacts are MISSING from the SOP that would be required for deployment of a high-risk AI system?
question.expected_answer: Missing: (1) AI system risk classification and conformity-assessment procedure (Article 43, Annex VI/VII), (2) fundamental-rights impact assessment for high-risk systems (Article 27, applicable to specific deployer categories), (3) EU database registration of the high-risk AI system (Article 49), (4) continuous risk-management system covering the lifecycle (Article 9 §2). Bias detection alone — though valuable — is one input to Article 10 data governance and does not substitute for the procedural requirements.
question.notes: Gap detection with specificity. Naive often lists what's there rather than what's missing.

output.answer:
Assuming SOP-AIML-009 is the governing procedure for EU deployment of a **high-risk AI system**, it is **not sufficient on its own** for EU AI Act deployment readiness. It is strong on bias testing, fairness metrics, remediation, and monitoring, but it is missing several **EU AI Act Article 9, 27, and 49** procedures and artefacts.

## Missing procedures / artefacts

| EU AI Act requirement | What SOP-AIML-009 covers | Missing from SOP-AIML-009 |
|---|---|---|
| **Article 9 — High-risk AI risk management system must be established, implemented, documented, maintained, and run as a continuous iterative lifecycle process** | SOP has a bias lifecycle: scoping, data preparation, validation, remediation, monitoring, and re-validation. See SOP §§5.1–5.6. | Missing a formal **EU AI Act High-Risk Risk Management File / Risk Management Plan** covering *all* risks to **health, safety, and fundamental rights**, not only algorithmic bias. Article 9(1)–(2) requires a documented lifecycle risk management system for high-risk AI systems. |
| **Article 9(2)(a) — Identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks when used as intended** | Bias Testing Plan identifies protected attributes and fairness metrics. SOP §5.1. | Missing a broader **hazard/risk register** for intended use risks, including clinical safety, financial harm, autonomy, privacy/fundamental rights, human oversight failure, robustness failure, and operational misuse. Article 9(2)(a). |
| **Article 9(2)(b) — Estimate and evaluate risks under reasonably foreseeable misuse** | SOP focuses on fairness failures and proxy variables. SOP §§5.2–5.5. | Missing a **foreseeable misuse assessment**: e.g., use outside intended population, overreliance by clinicians or lending staff, use without human review, use with degraded data, use by untrained deployers. Article 9(2)(b). |
| **Article 9(2)(c) — Evaluate risks from post-market monitoring data** | SOP has production bias monitoring and drift alerts. SOP §5.6. | Missing a procedure to feed **all post-market monitoring evidence** into the Article 9 risk management system, not just fairness metrics. Article 9(2)(c) refers to risks arising from post-market monitoring under Article 72. |
| **Article 9(2)(d), 9(5) — Adopt targeted risk controls and judge residual risk acceptable for each hazard and overall system** | SOP has remediation hierarchy for bias failures. SOP §5.5. | Missing **residual risk acceptance criteria**, documented risk-benefit rationale, and sign-off for each hazard and the overall system. SOP approval is based on `bias_governance: PASSED`, but Article 9(5) requires residual risk for each hazard and overall residual risk to be judged acceptable. |
| **Article 9(4) — Consider interaction among EU AI Act high-risk requirements** | SOP addresses bias, privacy consultation, human-in-the-loop, and monitoring separately. SOP §§4.3–4.4, 5.6. | Missing an **integrated requirements interaction assessment**, e.g., how fairness mitigation affects accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity, transparency, human oversight, and data governance. Article 9(4). |
| **Article 9(5)(c) — Provide required information and, where appropriate, training to deployers** | SOP has internal staff training. SOP §9. | Missing deployer-facing **instructions/training package** tied to identified risks, including limitations, human oversight instructions, escalation steps, and misuse warnings. Article 9(5)(c). |
| **Article 9(6)–(8) — Test high-risk AI systems to identify risk controls and verify compliance with high-risk requirements before placement/putting into service** | SOP requires fairness testing against predefined thresholds. SOP §§5.3–5.4. | Missing broader **Article 9 test protocol and report** demonstrating compliance beyond fairness, including safety, robustness, cybersecurity, human oversight, and intended-purpose performance. Article 9(6)–(8). |
| **Article 9(8) — Testing must use prior-defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds appropriate to intended purpose** | SOP defines fairness thresholds such as ±0.10 and 80% rule. SOP §§4.2, 5.1. | Missing intended-purpose **risk/performance thresholds** beyond bias metrics, such as clinical sensitivity/specificity floors, acceptable false-negative risk, operational failure thresholds, confidence thresholds, and override/error rates. Article 9(8). |
| **Article 9(9) — Consider adverse impact on persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups** | SOP lists age and disability as protected attributes. SOP §2. | Missing an explicit **children and vulnerable groups impact assessment**. Merely including age as a protected attribute does not satisfy Article 9(9)’s requirement to consider whether the system is likely to adversely affect persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups. |
| **Article 27 — Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment before deploying certain high-risk AI systems** | SOP has privacy consultation and references DPIAs where bias creates high risk. SOP §§3, 5.1, 10.1. | Missing a standalone **Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA)** procedure/template. Article 27(1) requires covered deployers to assess the fundamental rights impact before deployment. |
| **Article 27(1)(a) — Describe deployer processes in which the system will be used** | SOP requires PRD decision context. SOP §5.1. | Missing FRIA artefact section describing the **deployer’s operational process**, workflow, decision points, and how the AI system is used in line with intended purpose. Article 27(1)(a). |
| **Article 27(1)(b) — Describe period and frequency of use** | Not addressed in SOP. | Missing FRIA fields for **deployment duration, frequency of use, user groups, scale, and expected volume of decisions/predictions**. Article 27(1)(b). |
| **Article 27(1)(c) — Identify categories of natural persons and groups likely affected** | SOP identifies protected attributes for bias testing. SOP §§2, 5.1. | Missing a broader **affected-persons mapping** covering all categories of individuals and groups affected in the specific deployment context, not only protected attributes used for fairness metrics. Article 27(1)(c). |
| **Article 27(1)(d) — Identify specific risks of harm to those persons/groups, taking into account provider Article 13 information** | SOP assesses bias risk and disparate impact. SOP §§4.2, 5.3–5.5. | Missing FRIA analysis of **specific fundamental-rights harms** and explicit use of provider-supplied instructions/information. Article 27(1)(d) requires considering information given by the provider under Article 13. |
| **Article 27(1)(e) — Describe implementation of human oversight according to instructions for use** | SOP mandates human-in-the-loop for High/Critical decisions. SOP §4.3. | Missing deployment-specific **human oversight implementation record** linked to the provider’s instructions for use: reviewer role, competence, override rights, escalation, review sampling, and evidence of training. Article 27(1)(e). |
| **Article 27(1)(f) — Measures if risks materialise, including internal governance and complaint mechanisms** | SOP has bias incident escalation and ServiceNow P0 incidents. SOP §§5.6, 8.3. | Missing **complaint mechanism** for affected persons and FRIA-specific risk materialisation plan. SOP has internal incident escalation, but Article 27(1)(f) specifically requires arrangements including internal governance and complaint mechanisms. |
| **Article 27(2) — Update FRIA if elements change or become outdated** | SOP updates Model Cards and performs periodic bias revalidation. SOP §§4.5, 5.6. | Missing **FRIA update trigger and review cadence** for changes in use context, affected groups, risks, oversight measures, or complaint arrangements. Article 27(2). |
| **Article 27(3) — Notify market surveillance authority of FRIA results using the template** | Not addressed. | Missing **market surveillance authority notification procedure**, including owner, timing, completed template, submission evidence, and deployment gate. Article 27(3). |
| **Article 27(4) — FRIA complements DPIA where DPIA already covers obligations** | SOP references DPIAs and privacy consultation. SOP §§3, 5.1, 10.1. | Missing procedure explaining how the **FRIA complements, cross-references, or reuses DPIA content** without treating DPIA as a substitute. Article 27(4). |
| **Article 49 — Registration in EU database before placing on the market or putting into service** | No EU AI Act database registration control appears in SOP. | Missing **EU database registration procedure** for the provider or authorised representative before placing the high-risk AI system on the EU market or putting it into service. Article 49; see also EU AI Act Article 49 source: https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/49 |
| **Article 49 / Article 26(8) — Public authority deployers must comply with registration obligations and must not use an unregistered system** | SOP has vendor fairness certification but no EU registration check. SOP §6.2 A-03. | Missing deployer-side **registration verification gate**, especially for public authorities or Union bodies: check EU database registration before use, block use if not registered, and notify provider/distributor. Article 26(8) refers to Article 49 registration obligations. |
| **Article 49 — Registration information / evidence** | Not addressed. | Missing artefacts such as **EU database registration ID, submitted Annex VIII information package, registration owner, registration date, version linkage, and proof of registration retained in the model registry**. Article 49. |

## Bottom line

SOP-AIML-009 is a good **bias governance SOP**, but it is missing the deployment-critical EU AI Act artefacts for a high-risk AI system:

1. **Article 9 High-Risk AI Risk Management File** covering health, safety, fundamental rights, foreseeable misuse, residual risk, vulnerable groups, and full lifecycle testing.  
2. **Article 27 Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment** with required content, update triggers, complaint mechanisms, and notification to the market surveillance authority.  
3. **Article 49 EU Database Registration Procedure** with registration evidence and a deployment gate preventing EU use before registration.

Compliance level: partial

### Article 9: Risk Management System

1. A risk management system shall be established, implemented, documented and maintained in relation to high-risk AI systems.

2. The risk management system shall be understood as a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of a high-risk AI system, requiring regular systematic review and updating. It shall comprise the following steps:

(c) the evaluation of other risks possibly arising, based on the analysis of data gathered from the post-market monitoring system referred to in Article 72;

(d) the adoption of appropriate and targeted risk management measures designed to address the risks identified pursuant to point (a).

3. The risks referred to in this Article shall concern only those which may be reasonably mitigated or eliminated through the development or design of the high-risk AI system, or the provision of adequate technical information.

4. The risk management measures referred to in paragraph 2, point (d), shall give due consideration to the effects and possible interaction resulting from the combined application of the requirements set out in this Section, with a view to minimising risks more effectively while achieving an appropriate balance in implementing the measures to fulfil those requirements.

5. The risk management measures referred to in paragraph 2, point (d), shall be such that the relevant residual risk associated with each hazard, as well as the overall residual risk of the high-risk AI systems is judged to be acceptable. In identifying the most appropriate risk management measures, the following shall be ensured:

(a) elimination or reduction of risks identified and evaluated pursuant to paragraph 2 in as far as technically feasible through adequate design and development of the high-risk AI system;

(b) where appropriate, implementation of adequate mitigation and control measures addressing risks that cannot be eliminated;

(c) provision of information required pursuant to Article 13 and, where appropriate, training to deployers.

**Article 15: Accuracy, Robustness and Cybersecurity**
### Article 15: Accuracy, Robustness and Cybersecurity

1. High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.

2. To address the technical aspects of how to measure the appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness set out in paragraph 1 and any other relevant performance metrics, the Commission shall, in cooperation with relevant stakeholders and organisations such as metrology and benchmarking authorities, encourage, as appropriate, the development of benchmarks and measurement methodologies.

3. The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics of high-risk AI systems shall be declared in the accompanying instructions of use.

4. High-risk AI systems shall be as resilient as possible regarding errors, faults or inconsistencies that may occur within the system or the environment in which the system operates, in particular due to their interaction with natural persons or other systems. Technical and organisational measures shall be taken in this regard.

The robustness of high-risk AI systems may be achieved through technical redundancy solutions, which may include backup or fail-safe plans.

High-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or put into service shall be developed in such a way as to eliminate or reduce as far as possible the risk of possibly biased outputs influencing input for future operations (feedback loops), and as to ensure that any such feedback loops are duly addressed with appropriate mitigation measures.

5. High-risk AI systems shall be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities. The technical solutions aiming to ensure the cybersecurity of high-risk AI systems shall be appropriate to the relevant circumstances and the risks.

The technical solutions to address AI specific vulnerabilities shall include, where appropriate, measures to prevent, detect, respond to, resolve and control for attacks trying to manipulate the training data set (data poisoning), or pre-trained components used in training (model poisoning), inputs designed to cause the AI model to make a mistake (adversarial examples or model evasion), confidentiality attacks or model flaws.

---

**Article 27: Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment for High-Risk AI Systems**
### Article 27: Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment for High-Risk AI Systems (continued)

(a) it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks;

(b) based on a decision of the Commission, ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, it has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those set out in point (a) having regard to the criteria set out in Annex XIII.

2. A general-purpose AI model shall be presumed to have high impact capabilities pursuant to paragraph 1, point (a), when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training measured in floating point operations is greater than 10^25.

3. The Commission shall adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 to amend the thresholds listed in paragraphs 1 and 2 of this Article, as well as to supplement benchmarks and indicators in light of evolving technological developments, such as algorithmic improvements or increased hardware efficiency, when necessary, for these thresholds to reflect the state of the art.

## Article 52: Procedure

1. Where a general-purpose AI model meets the condition referred to in Article 51(1), point (a), the relevant provider shall notify the Commission without delay and in any event within two weeks after that requirement is met or it becomes known that it will be met. That notification shall include the information necessary to demonstrate that the relevant requirement has been met. If the Commission becomes aware of a general-purpose AI model presenting systemic risks of which it has not been notified, it may decide to designate it as a model with systemic risk.

2. The provider of a general-purpose AI model that meets the condition referred to in Article 51(1), point (a), may present, with its notification, sufficiently substantiated arguments to demonstrate that, exceptionally, although it meets that requirement, the general-purpose AI model does not present, due to its specific characteristics, systemic risks and therefore should not be classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk.

3. Where the Commission concludes that the arguments submitted pursuant to paragraph 2 are not sufficiently substantiated and the relevant provider was not able to demonstrate that the general-purpose AI model does not present, due to its specific characteristics, systemic risks, it shall reject those arguments, and the general-purpose AI model shall be considered to be a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk.

**Article 9: Risk Management System**
### Article 9: Risk Management System (continued)

With a view to eliminating or reducing risks related to the use of the high-risk AI system, due consideration shall be given to the technical knowledge, experience, education, the training to be expected by the deployer, and the presumable context in which the system is intended to be used.

6. High-risk AI systems shall be tested for the purpose of identifying the most appropriate and targeted risk management measures. Testing shall ensure that high-risk AI systems perform consistently for their intended purpose and that they are in compliance with the requirements set out in this Section.

7. Testing procedures may include testing in real-world conditions in accordance with Article 60.

8. The testing of high-risk AI systems shall be performed, as appropriate, at any time throughout the development process, and, in any event, prior to their being placed on the market or put into service. Testing shall be carried out against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds that are appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system.

9. When implementing the risk management system as provided for in paragraphs 1 to 7, providers shall give consideration to whether in view of its intended purpose the high-risk AI system is likely to have an adverse impact on persons under the age of 18 and, as appropriate, other vulnerable groups.

10. For providers of high-risk AI systems that are subject to requirements regarding internal risk management processes under other relevant provisions of Union law, the aspects provided in paragraphs 1 to 9 may be part of, or combined with, the risk management procedures established pursuant to that law.

### Article 11: Technical Documentation

1. The technical documentation of a high-risk AI system shall be drawn up before that system is placed on the market or put into service and shall be kept up-to date. 2. ### Article 26: Obligations of Deployers of High-Risk AI Systems (continued)

## Article 5: Prohibited AI Practices

1. The following AI practices shall be prohibited:

(a) the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, with the objective, or the effect of materially distorting the behaviour of a person or a group of persons by appreciably impairing their ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing them to take a decision that they would not have otherwise taken in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause that person, another person or group of persons significant harm;

(c) the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of AI systems for the evaluation or classification of natural persons or groups of persons over a certain period of time based on their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics, with the social score leading to either or both of the following:

(i) detrimental or unfavourable treatment of certain natural persons or groups of persons in social contexts that are unrelated to the contexts in which the data was originally generated or collected;
