Attributes of the AI RMF
NIST described several key attributes of the AI RMF when work on the Framework first
began. These attributes have remained intact and were used to guide the AI RMF’s devel-
opment. They are provided here as a reference.
The AI RMF strives to:
1. Be risk-based, resource-efficient, pro-innovation, and voluntary.
2. Be consensus-driven and developed and regularly updated through an open, trans-
parent process. All stakeholders should have the opportunity to contribute to the AI
RMF’s development.
3. Use clear and plain language that is understandable by a broad audience, including
senior executives, government officials, non-governmental organization leadership,
and those who are not AI professionals – while still of sufficient technical depth to
be useful to practitioners. The AI RMF should allow for communication of AI risks
across an organization, between organizations, with customers, and to the public at
large.
4. Provide common language and understanding to manage AI risks. The AI RMF
should offer taxonomy, terminology, definitions, metrics, and characterizations for
AI risk.
5. Be easily usable and fit well with other aspects of risk management. Use of the
Framework should be intuitive and readily adaptable as part of an organization’s
broader risk management strategy and processes. It should be consistent or aligned
with other approaches to managing AI risks.
6. Be useful to a wide range of perspectives, sectors, and technology domains. The AI
RMF should be universally applicable to any AI technology and to context-specific
use cases.
7. Be outcome-focused and non-prescriptive. The Framework should provide a catalog
of outcomes and approaches rather than prescribe one-size-fits-all requirements.
8. Take advantage of and foster greater awareness of existing standards, guidelines, best
practices, methodologies, and tools for managing AI risks – as well as illustrate the
need for additional, improved resources.
9. Be law- and regulation-agnostic. The Framework should support organizations’
abilities to operate under applicable domestic and international legal or regulatory
regimes.
10. Be a living document. The AI RMF should be readily updated as technology, under-
standing, and approaches to AI trustworthiness and uses of AI change and as stake-
holders learn from implementing AI risk management generally and this framework
in particular.

The GOVERN function:

• outlines processes, documents, and organizational schemes that anticipate, identify,

• incorporates processes to assess potential impacts;
• provides a structure by which AI risk management functions can align with organi-

5.2 Map
The MAP function establishes the context to frame risks related to an AI system. The AI
lifecycle consists of many interdependent activities involving a diverse set of actors (See
Figure 3). In practice, AI actors in charge of one part of the process often do not have full
visibility or control over other parts and their associated contexts. The interdependencies
between these activities, and among the relevant AI actors, can make it difficult to reliably
anticipate impacts of AI systems. For example, early decisions in identifying purposes and
objectives of an AI system can alter its behavior and capabilities, and the dynamics of de-
ployment setting (such as end users or impacted individuals) can shape the impacts of AI
system decisions. As a result, the best intentions within one dimension of the AI lifecycle
can be undermined via interactions with decisions and conditions in other, later activities.

NIST AI 100-1 AI RMF 1.0 1.2.2 Risk Tolerance While the AI RMF can be used to prioritize risk, it does not prescribe risk tolerance. Risk tolerance refers to the organization’s or AI actor’s (see Appendix A) readiness to bear the risk in order to achieve its objectives. Risk tolerance can be influenced by legal or regula- tory requirements (Adapted from: ISO GUIDE 73). Risk tolerance and the level of risk that is acceptable to organizations or society are highly contextual and application and use-case specific. Risk tolerances can be influenced by policies and norms established by AI sys- tem owners, organizations, industries, communities, or policy makers. Risk tolerances are likely to change over time as AI systems, policies, and norms evolve. Different organiza- tions may have varied risk tolerances due to their particular organizational priorities and resource considerations. Emerging knowledge and methods to better inform harm/cost-benefit tradeoffs will con- tinue to be developed and debated by businesses, governments, academia, and civil society. To the extent that challenges for specifying AI risk tolerances remain unresolved, there may be contexts where a risk management framework is not yet readily applicable for mitigating negative AI risks. The Framework is intended to be flexible and to augment existing risk practices which should align with applicable laws, regulations, and norms. Organizations should follow existing regulations and guidelines for risk criteria, tolerance, and response established by organizational, domain, discipline, sector, or professional requirements. Some sectors or industries may have established definitions of harm or established documentation, reporting, and disclosure requirements. Within sectors, risk management may depend on existing guidelines for specific applications and use case settings. Where established guidelines do not exist, organizations should define reasonable risk tolerance. Once tolerance is defined, this AI RMF can be used to manage risks and to document risk management processes. 1.2.3 Risk Prioritization Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully. Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. NIST AI 100-1 AI RMF 1.0 Executive Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have significant potential to transform society and people’s lives – from commerce and health to transportation and cybersecurity to the envi- ronment and our planet. AI technologies can drive inclusive economic growth and support scientific advancements that improve the conditions of our world. AI technologies, how- ever, also pose risks that can negatively impact individuals, groups, organizations, commu- nities, society, the environment, and the planet. Like risks for other types of technology, AI risks can emerge in a variety of ways and can be characterized as long- or short-term, high- or low-probability, systemic or localized, and high- or low-impact. The AI RMF refers to an AI system as an engineered or machine-based system that can, for a given set of objectives, generate outputs such as predictions, recommenda- tions, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments. AI systems are designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy (Adapted from: OECD Recommendation on AI:2019; ISO /IEC 22989:2022). While there are myriad standards and best practices to help organizations mitigate the risks of traditional software or information-based systems, the risks posed by AI systems are in many ways unique (See Appendix B). AI systems, for example, may be trained on data that can change over time, sometimes significantly and unexpectedly, affecting system function- ality and trustworthiness in ways that are hard to understand. AI systems and the contexts in which they are deployed are frequently complex, making it difficult to detect and respond to failures when they occur. AI systems are inherently socio-technical in nature, meaning they are influenced by societal dynamics and human behavior. AI risks – and benefits – can emerge from the interplay of technical aspects combined with societal factors related to how a system is used, its interactions with other AI systems, who operates it, and the social context in which it is deployed. These risks make AI a uniquely challenging technology to deploy and utilize both for orga- nizations and within society. Without proper controls, AI systems can amplify, perpetuate, or exacerbate inequitable or undesirable outcomes for individuals and communities. With proper controls, AI systems can mitigate and manage inequitable outcomes. AI risk management is a key component of responsible development and use of AI sys- tems. Responsible AI practices can help align the decisions about AI system design, de- velopment, and uses with intended aim and values. Core concepts in responsible AI em- phasize human centricity, social responsibility, and sustainability. AI risk management can drive responsible uses and practices by

Privacy values such as anonymity, confidentiality, and control generally should guide choices for AI system design, development, and deployment. Privacy-enhancing technologies (“PETs”) for AI, as well as data minimizing methods such as de-identification and aggregation for certain model outputs, can support design for privacy-enhanced AI systems. NIST AI 100-1 AI RMF 1.0 Appendix A: Descriptions of AI Actor Tasks from Figures 2 and 3 AI Design tasks are performed during the Application Context and Data and Input phases of the AI lifecycle in Figure 2. AI Design actors create the concept and objectives of AI systems and are responsible for the planning, design, and data collection and processing tasks of the AI system so that the AI system is lawful and fit-for-purpose. Tasks include ar- ticulating and documenting the system’s concept and objectives, underlying assumptions, context, and requirements; gathering and cleaning data; and documenting the metadata and characteristics of the dataset. AI actors in this category include data scientists, do- main experts, socio-cultural analysts, experts in the field of diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility, members of impacted communities, human factors experts (e.g., UX/UI design), governance experts, data engineers, data providers, system funders, product man- agers, third-party entities, evaluators, and legal and privacy governance. AI Development tasks are performed during the AI Model phase of the lifecycle in Figure 2. AI Development actors provide the initial infrastructure of AI systems and are responsi- ble for model building and interpretation tasks, which involve the creation, selection, cali- bration, training, and/or testing of models or algorithms. AI actors in this category include machine learning experts, data scientists, developers, third-party entities, legal and privacy governance experts, and experts in the socio-cultural and contextual factors associated with the deployment setting. AI Deployment tasks are performed during the Task and Output phase of the lifecycle in Figure 2. AI Deployment actors are responsible for contextual decisions relating to how the AI system is used to assure deployment of the system into production. Related tasks include piloting the system, checking compatibility with legacy systems, ensuring regu- latory compliance, managing organizational change, and evaluating user experience. AI actors in this category include system integrators, software developers, end users, oper- ators and practitioners, evaluators, and domain experts with expertise in human factors, socio-cultural analysis, and governance. Operation and Monitoring tasks are performed in the Application Context/Operate and Monitor phase of the lifecycle in Figure 2. These tasks are carried out by AI actors who are responsible for operating the AI system and working with others to regularly assess system output and impacts. Overview of Risks Unique to or Exacerbated by GAI In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability (or likelihood) of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event. Some risks can be assessed as likely to materialize in a given context, particularly those that have been empirically demonstrated in similar contexts. Other risks may be unlikely to materialize in a given context, or may be more speculative and therefore uncertain. AI risks can diﬀer from or intensify traditional software risks. Likewise, GAI can exacerbate existing AI risks, and creates unique risks. GAI risks can vary along many dimensions: • Stage of the AI lifecycle: Risks can arise during design, development, deployment, operation, and/or decommissioning. • Scope: Risks may exist at individual model or system levels, at the application or implementation levels (i.e., for a speciﬁc use case), or at the ecosystem level – that is, beyond a single system or organizational context. Examples of the latter include the expansion of “algorithmic monocultures,3” resulting from repeated use of the same model, or impacts on access to opportunity, labor markets, and the creative economies.4 • Source of risk: Risks may emerge from factors related to the design, training, or operation of the GAI model itself, stemming in some cases from GAI model or system inputs, and in other cases, from GAI system outputs. Responsible use and practice of AI systems is a counterpart to AI system trustworthiness. AI systems are not inherently bad or risky, and it is often the contextual environment that determines whether or not negative impact will occur. The AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) can help organizations enhance their understanding of how the contexts in which the AI systems they build and deploy may interact with and affect individuals, groups, and communities. Responsible AI use and practice can: » assist AI designers, developers, deployers, evaluators, and users to think more critically about context and potential or unexpected negative and positive impacts; » be leveraged to design, develop, evaluate, and use AI systems with impact in mind; and » prevent, preempt, detect, mitigate, and manage AI risks. 1.2. Purpose of the AI RMF Cultivating trust by understanding and managing the risks of AI systems will help preserve civil liberties and rights, and enhance safety while creating opportunities for innovation and realizing the full potential of this technology. The AI RMF is intended to address challenges unique to AI systems and encourage and equip different AI stakeholders to manage AI risks proactively and purposefully. question.question: Reviewing SOP-CLIN-001 (Clinical Decision Support System Validation) against EU AI Act Article 11 (technical documentation) and Article 17 (quality management system), what's MISSING from the SOP?
question.expected_answer: Missing: (1) coverage of all Annex IV documentation elements — general description, design specifications, system architecture, training/testing/validation data and methodology, post-market monitoring plan, declaration of conformity, instructions for use; (2) explicit linkage between the QMS components and Article 17 sub-elements — regulatory compliance strategy, design control, data management, technical documentation, post-market monitoring system (Article 72), incident reporting (Article 73), communication with authorities, record-keeping, resource management; (3) traceability matrix mapping each Annex IV / Article 17 element to specific SOPs or evidence artifacts; (4) responsible roles for each QMS element.

output.answer:
Assuming SOP-CLIN-001 governs high-risk CDSS products, it is **strong on clinical validation execution**, but it is **not a complete EU AI Act Article 11 technical-documentation procedure or Article 17 QMS procedure**. The main missing items are below.

## Missing against Article 11 — Technical documentation

| Gap | What’s missing from SOP-CLIN-001 | EU AI Act basis |
|---|---|---|
| **1. No explicit technical documentation lifecycle** | The SOP says the Final Validation Report “includes all Annex IV documentation elements” but does not require a controlled **technical documentation file** to be drawn up **before** placing on the market / putting into service, maintained, versioned, and kept up to date after changes. | Article 11(1): technical documentation must be drawn up before market/put-into-service and kept up to date. |
| **2. No Annex IV checklist / required contents** | The SOP does not enumerate the mandatory Annex IV contents or require an Annex IV traceability matrix showing where each element is satisfied. A blanket statement in §5.5 is insufficient. | Article 11(1): documentation must contain, at minimum, Annex IV elements. |
| **3. Missing full system description package** | SOP lacks mandatory documentation requirements for: provider identity/contact, system version and relation to prior versions, intended purpose, forms in which the AI system is placed on the market, hardware requirements, user interface, interaction with external software/hardware such as EHRs, and instructions for use as part of the technical file. | Article 11(1), Annex IV general system-description elements; Article 13(3)(a)-(f) for deployer-facing information. |
| **4. Missing design/development documentation** | SOP validates a frozen model but does not require technical documentation of development methods, design specifications, model logic, algorithms, architecture, key design assumptions, optimization objectives, pre-trained models used/integrated, or computational resources used for development/training/testing. | Article 11(1), Annex IV development-process and system-architecture elements. |
| **5. Incomplete dataset documentation** | SOP covers validation data lockbox and de-identification, but does not require full documentation for **training, validation, and testing datasets**, including provenance, scope, main characteristics, data selection, labelling, cleaning, gaps, representativeness, and suitability. | Article 10(2)-(4) requires data governance and representative/suitable datasets; Article 11(1), Annex IV requires dataset/data requirement documentation. |
| **6. Missing human oversight assessment** | SOP says CDSS is advisory and clinicians retain judgment, but does not require a documented Article 14 human-oversight assessment: oversight measures, ability to interpret outputs, avoid automation bias, override/disregard outputs, intervene/stop use, or training/information needed by deployers. | Article 11(1), Annex IV requires human oversight documentation; Article 14 sets human oversight expectations. |
| **7. Missing foreseeable misuse and fundamental-rights risk documentation** | SOP addresses clinical performance and subgroup fairness, but does not require documentation of foreseeable misuse, unintended outcomes, health/safety/fundamental-rights risks, residual risks, or mitigation traceability in the technical file. | Article 9(2) requires identifying/evaluating risks including reasonably foreseeable misuse and fundamental-rights risks; Article 11(1), Annex IV requires risk-management documentation. |
| **8. No product-specific harmonised standards / common specifications mapping** | SOP lists external standards generally, but does not require each CDSS technical file to identify harmonised standards or common specifications applied in full/part, or alternative means used where they are not applied. | Article 17(1)(e) requires technical specifications and standards; Article 11(1), Annex IV requires standards/solutions documentation. |
| **9. Cybersecurity documentation is incomplete** | SOP documents validation-environment controls and access logging, but does not require documentation/testing of the deployed AI system’s cybersecurity, robustness, and security measures. | Article 15 addresses accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity; Article 11(1), Annex IV requires cybersecurity measures in technical documentation. |
| **10. Post-market monitoring plan timing is wrong/incomplete** | SOP §7.1 says a PMCF/post-market plan must be filed **within 30 days of deployment**. For Article 11, the post-market monitoring plan must be part of the technical documentation before placing on market/putting into service. | Article 72(3): post-market monitoring plan is part of Annex IV technical documentation; Article 11(1): technical documentation exists before market/put-into-service. |
| **11. Missing EU Declaration of Conformity artifact** | SOP approval ends with CMO release authorization, but does not require an EU Declaration of Conformity to be included in the technical documentation package. | Article 16(g) requires EU declaration of conformity; Annex IV technical documentation includes conformity documentation. |
| **12. Missing single technical documentation set for MDR-covered CDSS** | SOP references EU MDR and CE-marked/FDA-cleared products, but does not require a **single technical documentation set** combining AI Act documentation with MDR documentation where the AI system is part of a product subject to Union harmonisation legislation. | Article 11(2): for high-risk AI systems related to products covered by listed Union harmonisation legislation, a single set of technical documentation must be drawn up. |

## Missing against Article 17 — Quality management system

| Gap | What’s missing from SOP-CLIN-001 | EU AI Act basis |
|---|---|---|
| **1. No complete AI Act regulatory compliance strategy** | SOP states “regulatory alignment,” but does not define a QMS strategy for AI Act compliance, conformity assessment, CE marking, EU declaration, registration, management of modifications, and regulatory responsibilities. | Article 17(1)(a) requires a regulatory compliance strategy, including conformity assessment and modification management. |
| **2. Design controls are not defined** | SOP starts at validation-study design and model freeze, but lacks design inputs/outputs, design reviews, design verification, requirements traceability, and design-control gates for CDSS design. | Article 17(1)(b) requires techniques/procedures/systematic actions for design, design control and design verification. |
| **3. Development QA/QC is not covered** | SOP refers to model execution and validation, but not software/model development quality control, code quality, peer review, secure SDLC, release QA, or development-stage acceptance criteria. | Article 17(1)(c) requires development, quality control and quality assurance procedures. |
| **4. Testing frequency before/during/after development is incomplete** | SOP requires pre-deployment validation and annual revalidation, but does not define test/validation procedures and frequency **before, during, and after development** across the full lifecycle. | Article 17(1)(d) requires examination, test and validation procedures before, during and after development and their frequency. |
| **5. Data management QMS is incomplete** | SOP covers validation lockbox data, de-identification, and annotation, but does not cover end-to-end data management for training and production lifecycle: acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation, retention, bias detection/mitigation, and data-gap remediation. | Article 17(1)(f) requires systems/procedures for data management; Article 10(2)-(4) specifies data governance expectations. |
| **6. Risk management system is only referenced, not operationalized** | SOP references SOP-CLIN-002 and FMEA, but does not embed required risk-management outputs, residual-risk acceptance, foreseeable misuse analysis, mitigation traceability, or risk review gates into this validation SOP. | Article 17(1)(g) requires the Article 9 risk management system; Article 9(1)-(5) requires lifecycle risk management, residual-risk acceptability and mitigation measures. |
| **7. Post-market monitoring system is partial** | SOP has KPIs and reporting cadence, but does not require a documented Article 72 post-market monitoring system that systematically collects, documents, and analyses performance data throughout lifetime to evaluate continued compliance, including interactions with other AI systems where relevant. | Article 17(1)(h) requires post-market monitoring; Article 72(1)-(3) defines the documented system and plan. |
| **8. Serious incident reporting process is missing** | SOP says findings are reported to regulatory bodies, but lacks Article 73 incident definitions, reportability criteria, timelines, competent-authority notification workflow, ownership, and records. | Article 17(1)(i) requires procedures for serious incident reporting; Article 73 governs reporting of serious incidents. |
| **9. External regulatory communications procedure is missing** | Regulatory Affairs is “consulted,” but SOP lacks a procedure for communications with national competent authorities, notified bodies, sectoral authorities, other operators, customers, and interested parties. | Article 17(1)(j) requires procedures for handling such communications. |
| **10. Recordkeeping inventory and retention are missing** | SOP stores signed artifacts and logs, but does not define a complete QMS/technical-documentation record inventory, retention period, location, access, retrieval, or authority-disclosure process. | Article 17(1)(k) requires record keeping of all relevant documentation and information; Article 18(1) requires keeping technical/QMS documentation available for 10 years. |
| **11. Resource management and supply continuity are missing** | SOP assigns validation roles and mentions resource allocation, but does not define QMS resource management, competence capacity, infrastructure, supplier continuity, compute/environment availability, or security-of-supply measures. | Article 17(1)(l) requires resource management, including security-of-supply-related measures. |
| **12. Accountability framework is limited to validation only** | The RACI covers validation activities, but not all Article 17 QMS aspects: regulatory strategy, design controls, development QA, data governance, risk management, post-market monitoring, incident reporting, recordkeeping, communications, and resources. | Article 17(1)(m) requires an accountability framework for management and staff responsibilities across all QMS aspects. |

## Bottom line

SOP-CLIN-001 is a good **clinical validation SOP**, but it is missing the procedural backbone needed to prove full EU AI Act Article 11 and Article 17 compliance. The largest gaps are: **Annex IV technical-documentation content control, full QMS coverage, conformity-assessment/regulatory strategy, design/development controls, lifecycle risk management, serious-incident reporting, record retention, and post-market monitoring timing.**

Compliance level: partial

scores.judge_rationale: The candidate answer comprehensively identifies all missing elements from the reference answer (Annex IV documentation coverage, Article 17 QMS sub-elements, traceability matrix, and responsible roles) with extensive additional detail, and correctly cites EU AI Act Article 11, Article 17, Annex IV, plus related articles (10, 13, 14, 15, 16, 18, 72, 73) that are directly relevant to the analysis.

question.question: Reviewing SOP-LEGC-005 (Regulatory Filing and Reporting) against GDPR's transparency and transfer obligations, what specific elements are MISSING?
question.expected_answer: Missing: (1) Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) or alternative Chapter V transfer mechanisms for cross-border filings — international transfers are acknowledged but the operational mechanism is not specified; (2) transfer-impact-assessment procedures considering the legal environment of recipient jurisdictions; (3) Article 13/14 specificity in privacy notices triggered by filing-related processing — purposes, lawful basis, recipients (regulators), retention, data-subject rights; (4) supplementary measures (encryption, pseudonymisation) tied to high-risk filings; (5) records of processing (Article 30) specifically for filing-related processing activities.

output.answer:
SOP-LEGC-005 is **missing several GDPR-specific transparency and international-transfer elements**. The SOP contains only a high-level statement that EU personal data in regulatory filings is handled under GDPR, that data subjects are informed through website privacy notices, and that “appropriate safeguards” are used for EU-to-US transfers. It does **not** operationalize the required GDPR content, timing, documentation, or transfer-mechanism controls.

## Missing GDPR transparency elements

1. **No procedure ensuring Article 12-compliant notice format and delivery**
   - GDPR requires information to be provided in a **concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form**, using **clear and plain language**, and to facilitate data subject rights requests.  
   - SOP-LEGC-005 only says notices are posted on the corporate website; it does not define readability, accessibility, delivery method, timing, or ownership controls for privacy-notice updates.  
   - Citation: GDPR Article 12.

2. **No required Article 13 notice-content checklist for data collected directly from individuals**
   The SOP does not require regulatory-filing privacy notices to include:
   - controller identity and contact details;
   - EU representative details, where applicable;
   - DPO contact details;
   - purposes of processing and legal basis;
   - legitimate interests, if relied upon;
   - recipients or categories of recipients, including regulators and internal teams;
   - retention period or retention criteria;
   - data subject rights;
   - right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority;
   - whether provision of data is statutory/contractual and consequences of not providing it;
   - automated decision-making/profiling information, where applicable.  
   - Citation: GDPR Article 13(1)–(2).

3. **No Article 14 notice-content checklist for data not obtained directly from the data subject**
   Regulatory filings may use data compiled from business systems, customers, partners, clinical operations, or analytics sources. The SOP does not require Article 14 disclosures such as:
   - categories of personal data concerned;
   - source of the personal data, including whether it came from publicly accessible sources;
   - the same controller/DPO/purpose/legal basis/recipient/retention/rights/complaint/automated-decision information required for indirect collection scenarios.  
   - Citation: GDPR Article 14(1)–(2).

4. **No Article 14 timing rules**
   The SOP does not specify when data subjects must receive notice where personal data is not obtained directly from them—e.g., within the GDPR timing framework, at first communication, or before disclosure where applicable.  
   - Citation: GDPR Article 14(3).

5. **No trigger for new or updated notice before further processing**
   The SOP does not require a privacy-notice update or data-subject communication when personal data collected for one purpose is later used for a different regulatory filing/reporting purpose. GDPR requires notice before further processing for a different purpose.  
   - Citation: GDPR Article 13(3); GDPR Article 14(4).

6. **No transparency control for disclosures to regulators as recipients**
   SOP-LEGC-005 defines “Regulatory Addressee” operationally, but does not require privacy notices or ROPA entries to describe regulators, supervisory authorities, public authorities, or other filing recipients as **recipients or categories of recipients**.  
   - Citation: GDPR Article 13(1)(e); GDPR Article 14(1)(e); GDPR Article 30(1)(d).

7. **No explicit link between regulatory filings and ROPA completeness**
   The SOP says the DPO owns GDPR-related submissions, including ROPA summaries when requested, but it does not require each regulatory filing involving personal data to be mapped to a ROPA entry covering purposes, data categories, data-subject categories, recipients, international transfers, retention, and security measures.  
   - Citation: GDPR Article 30(1).

## Missing GDPR international-transfer elements

1. **No identification of the specific transfer mechanism**
   The SOP says “appropriate safeguards are in place” for EU-to-US transfers, but does not require the filing owner to identify whether the transfer relies on:
   - adequacy decision;
   - Standard Contractual Clauses;
   - Binding Corporate Rules;
   - approved code of conduct;
   - certification mechanism;
   - contractual clauses authorized by a supervisory authority;
   - Article 49 derogation.  
   - Citation: GDPR Articles 45, 46, 47, and 49.

2. **No adequacy-decision check**
   The SOP does not require verification of whether the destination country, territory, sector, or international organization is covered by a European Commission adequacy decision before transfer.  
   - Citation: GDPR Article 45.

3. **No Article 46 safeguard documentation**
   Where there is no adequacy decision, GDPR permits transfers only if appropriate safeguards are provided and enforceable data-subject rights and effective legal remedies are available. The SOP does not require documenting those safeguards for each regulatory-filing transfer.  
   - Citation: GDPR Article 46(1).

4. **No requirement to make safeguards available to data subjects**
   GDPR requires transparency notices to state the existence or absence of an adequacy decision and, for Article 46/47 or certain Article 49 transfers, reference the safeguards and the means to obtain a copy or where they are available. SOP-LEGC-005 does not require that language in notices.  
   - Citation: GDPR Article 13(1)(f); GDPR Article 14(1)(f).

5. **No controls for onward transfers**
   The SOP addresses EU-to-US transfers to Meridian analytics teams, but not onward transfers from those teams to vendors, affiliates, regulators, consultants, external counsel, cloud providers, or other third-country recipients. Binding Corporate Rules must address onward transfers to entities not bound by the rules, and Article 46 transfers require enforceable rights and remedies.  
   - Citation: GDPR Article 46(1); GDPR Article 47(2).

6. **No Article 49 derogation governance**
   The SOP does not define when derogations may be used, how explicit consent is obtained if relied on, how “important public interest” or “legal claims” is assessed, or how exceptional transfers are documented.  
   - Citation: GDPR Article 49(1).

7. **No process for exceptional non-repetitive transfers based on compelling legitimate interests**
   GDPR allows this only under narrow conditions, including assessment of circumstances, suitable safeguards, supervisory-authority notice, and informing data subjects of the transfer and compelling legitimate interests. SOP-LEGC-005 contains no such workflow.  
   - Citation: GDPR Article 49(1), second subparagraph.

8. **No ROPA transfer fields embedded in the filing workflow**
   GDPR requires records of processing to include transfers to third countries or international organizations, identification of the third country/international organization, and documentation of suitable safeguards for certain Article 49 transfers. SOP-LEGC-005’s filing metadata includes Obligation ID, Regulator, Report Type, Date of Submission, and Legal Hold Flag, but not transfer country, mechanism, safeguards, or onward-transfer details.  
   - Citation: GDPR Article 30(1)(e); GDPR Article 30(2)(c).

## Bottom line

SOP-LEGC-005 has a **general GDPR statement**, but it is missing the operational controls needed to demonstrate GDPR transparency and transfer compliance for regulatory filings: required notice content, notice timing, recipient disclosures, transfer-mechanism selection, safeguard documentation, data-subject access to safeguard information, onward-transfer controls, derogation governance, and ROPA integration.

Compliance level: partial

scores.judge_rationale: The candidate answer is comprehensive and fully correct, identifying all five missing elements from the reference (SCCs/transfer mechanisms, transfer impact assessment, Article 13/14 specificity, supplementary measures, and Article 30 ROPA records) plus additional valid points; however, while it cites Articles 13, 14, and 30 correctly, it fails to cite Chapter V as a whole (the expected citation for transfer obligations) and instead cites individual articles 45, 46, 47, 49, missing the broader Chapter V reference.

question.question: Reviewing SOP-ITOP-005 (Capacity Planning and Management) against SOC 2 Common Criteria CC7 (monitoring) and CC8 (change management), what specific controls are MISSING?
question.expected_answer: Missing: (1) scheduled tabletop exercises for incident-response scenarios (CC7.4) — the plan exists but periodic testing is absent; (2) defined alert thresholds and escalation paths for capacity-related anomalies (CC7.2/7.3); (3) explicit segregation of duties between change requester, approver, and implementer for capacity changes (CC8.1); (4) post-incident review procedures feeding lessons learned back to monitoring and change processes (CC7.5).

output.answer:
Below are the **specific missing controls** in SOP-ITOP-005 when reviewed against **SOC 2 Common Criteria CC7 monitoring** and **CC8 change management**.

## Missing CC7 monitoring controls

| SOC 2 requirement | What SOP-ITOP-005 has | Missing control |
|---|---|---|
| **CC7.1 — Detection and monitoring procedures to identify configuration changes that introduce vulnerabilities and susceptibilities to newly discovered vulnerabilities.** Points of focus include defined configuration standards, monitoring infrastructure/software for noncompliance, change-detection mechanisms, detecting unauthorized components, and vulnerability scans periodically and after significant changes. | SOP-ITOP-005 monitors capacity/performance metrics such as CPU, memory, disk I/O, network throughput, latency, error rate, Kafka lag, and DB pool utilization; see SOP §§5.1–5.2. | **No control requiring hardened configuration standards or monitoring for configuration drift/noncompliance** after capacity changes. The SOP has performance baselines, but not security/configuration baselines. SOC 2 CC7.1 specifically expects defined configuration standards and monitoring for noncompliance. |
| **CC7.1 — Implements change-detection mechanisms, such as file integrity monitoring, to alert personnel to unauthorized modifications of critical system files, configuration files, or content files.** | SOP relies on IaC, GitHub branch protection, CODEOWNERS, ServiceNow, and CloudTrail for manual AWS changes; see SOP §§5.4, 6.1, 6.2. | **No explicit file/configuration integrity monitoring or unauthorized modification alerting** for critical files, configuration files, infrastructure manifests, Helm values, Terraform state/configuration, or content files. |

| **CC7.1 — Conducts infrastructure and software vulnerability scans periodically and after significant changes; deficiencies are remediated timely.** | SOP addresses capacity monitoring and post-incident capacity reviews; see SOP §§5.2, 5.5. | **No vulnerability scanning requirement after significant capacity changes**, such as new EC2 instances, Kubernetes nodes, database replicas, Kafka partitions, GPU endpoints, or Terraform/Helm changes. | **CC7.2 — Monitors system components for anomalies indicative of malicious acts, natural disasters, and errors; anomalies are analyzed to determine whether they represent security events.** Points of focus include detection policies/tools for intrusions, inappropriate access, unusual system activity, anomaly filtering/summarization/analysis, and monitoring detection tools for effective operation. | SOP monitors operational capacity anomalies and SLO breaches; see SOP §§4.2, 5.2. | **Monitoring is capacity-centric, not security-event-centric.** The SOP does not define detection logic for intrusions, inappropriate access, compromised credentials, unauthorized external access, malicious activity, or natural-disaster indicators as required by SOC 2 CC7.2. |
| **CC7.2 — Implements filters to analyze anomalies and identify security events.** | SOP defines threshold tiers and incident creation for capacity breaches; see SOP §5.2. | **No documented triage/filtering process to determine whether capacity anomalies are security events**, such as DDoS, credential abuse, crypto-mining, unauthorized data export, bot traffic, or compromised workload behavior. |
| **CC7.2 — Monitors and maintains effectiveness of detection tools.** | SOP uses Datadog, synthetic checks, PagerDuty, ServiceNow, and CloudTrail-related alerting; see SOP §§5.2, 6.1, 7.2. | **No control requiring periodic testing/tuning of monitoring and alerting tools** to confirm Datadog monitors, synthetic checks, PagerDuty routing, ServiceNow ticket creation, CloudTrail/Security Hub alerts, and dead-man switches operate effectively. |
| **CC7.3 — Evaluates security events to determine whether they are security incidents and takes action; response procedures are evaluated periodically.** | SOP says capacity-related SLO breaches are incidents and managed under SOP-ISEC-002; PIRs are required for P1/P2 capacity incidents; see SOP §§4.5, 5.5. | **No periodic exercise/testing control for capacity-related incident response.** The SOP explicitly states that regular tabletop exercises are not currently scheduled; see SOP §4.5. SOC 2 CC7.3 expects response procedures to be evaluated periodically. |
| **CC7.3 — Detected security events are communicated to and reviewed by individuals responsible for the security program.** | ISO is consulted on security implications and incident coordination; see SOP §3. | **No mandatory ISO/security-team review trigger for capacity anomalies that may indicate security events.** The SOP involves ISO for some security implications, but does not require security review of suspicious capacity anomalies before closing incidents. |

## Missing CC8 change management controls

| SOC 2 requirement | What SOP-ITOP-005 has | Missing control |
|---|---|---|
| **CC8.1 — Changes to infrastructure, data, software, and procedures are authorized, designed/developed/acquired, configured, documented, tested, approved, and implemented.** | SOP requires production capacity changes to be authorized via ServiceNow and approved per SOP-CHG-001; see SOP §4.4. Vertical scaling requires a CHG, rollback plan, stakeholder communication, and approvals; see SOP §5.4.2. | **Horizontal scaling runbook lacks explicit ServiceNow Change Request creation before implementation.** SOP §5.4.1 uses PR approval and later updates the ServiceNow Incident/Alert, but does not require a CHG before horizontal scaling, despite SOP §4.4 stating any production capacity change must have a Change Request. |
| **CC8.1 — Tracks system changes prior to implementation.** | Vertical scaling creates a CHG before implementation; see SOP §5.4.2. | **Forecast-driven and horizontal scaling changes are not consistently tracked as changes before production implementation.** SOP §5.4.1 tracks via Git PR, but does not require ServiceNow CHG tracking before implementation. |
| **CC8.1 — Tests system changes prior to implementation into production.** Examples include unit, integration, regression, QA, static/dynamic testing, or automated testing. | SOP requires `terraform plan` or `helm diff` output and post-change validation that new instances register and thresholds subside; see SOP §5.4.1. | **No pre-production testing requirement for capacity changes.** `terraform plan`/`helm diff` are impact previews, not sufficient evidence of functional, integration, regression, performance, security, or rollback testing before production deployment under SOC 2 CC8.1. |
| **CC8.1 — Documents system changes to support ongoing maintenance and internal/external users.** | SOP requires PRs, ServiceNow incidents/alerts, and CHG for vertical scaling; see SOP §§5.4.1–5.4.2. | **No consistent required change documentation package for all capacity changes.** Horizontal scaling only requires updating the incident/alert with action taken; it does not require a complete CHG record with business justification, risk, affected services, test evidence, implementation steps, rollback, validation, and approvals. |

| **CC8.1 — Creates and maintains baseline configuration of IT technology.** | SOP creates performance baselines; see SOP §5.1. | **No baseline configuration control.** Performance baselines are not the same as approved configuration baselines for infrastructure, software, network, Kubernetes, database, Terraform, Helm, or cloud service settings. |
| **CC8.1 — Provides for emergency changes, including authorizing, designing, testing, approving, and implementing emergency changes.** | SOP has exception handling and escalation, including emergency spend and override of standard change lead times; see SOP §§8.1–8.3. | **No complete emergency change-management workflow.** The SOP does not define emergency change authorization, minimum testing, approval path, implementation evidence, post-implementation review, or retrospective approval requirements for urgent capacity changes. |
| **CC8.1 — Configures software by selecting, implementing, maintaining, and monitoring configuration parameters used to control functionality.** | SOP modifies Terraform modules and Helm values for scaling; see SOP §5.4. | **No configuration parameter governance for capacity-related software/cloud settings.** The SOP does not require approved parameter ranges, configuration owners, periodic review of autoscaling limits, database parameters, Kafka partition settings, Kubernetes resource limits, or monitoring that parameters remain within approved baselines. |
| **CC8.1 — Identifies changes in infrastructure, data, software, and procedures required to remediate incidents and initiates the change process.** | SOP requires PIR action items in Jira after P1/P2 capacity incidents; see SOP §5.5. | **PIR action items are not explicitly tied to the formal change process.** The SOP requires Jira actions, but does not require that remediation changes be converted into ServiceNow Change Requests and managed through authorization, testing, approval, and implementation under CC8.1. |

## Bottom line

SOP-ITOP-005 is reasonably strong for **capacity monitoring and basic IaC-based approval**, but it is missing several SOC 2 controls because it treats monitoring and changes primarily as **performance/capacity activities**, not as full **security monitoring and formal change-management controls**.

The most important gaps are:

1. No security-focused anomaly detection and triage for capacity events.  
2. No vulnerability scanning after significant capacity changes.  
3. No configuration drift/file integrity/unauthorized component detection.  
4. No periodic testing of monitoring/detection tools.  
5. No scheduled tabletop or periodic evaluation of capacity incident response.  
6. Horizontal scaling lacks explicit pre-implementation ServiceNow CHG control.

The trust services criteria set forth the outcomes that an entity’s controls should ordinarily meet to 
achieve the entity’s unique objectives. Therefore, the trust services criteria are intended to be used for 
evaluation and reporting, regardless of the specific controls implemented by management. This contrasts 
with the approach taken by process and controls frameworks, which mandate that the entity implement a 
specific set of controls. The trust services criteria recognize that there is no specific set of processes and 
controls that can effectively mitigate all the unique threats, vulnerabilities, and risks that entities face. 
Instead, each entity is responsible for establishing its own objectives, assessing the unique risks that 
threaten the achievement of those objectives, and implementing processes and controls to mitigate those 
risks to acceptable levels. Because each entity is unique, applying the trust services criteria in actual sit-
uations requires judgment.

question.question: Reviewing SOP-LEGC-005 (Regulatory Filing and Reporting) against HIPAA's breach-reporting and de-identification requirements, what specific elements are MISSING?
question.expected_answer: Missing: (1) de-identification methodology for PHI appearing in filings — neither Safe Harbor (§164.514(b)(2)) nor Expert Determination (§164.514(b)(1)) is specified; (2) breach-notification procedures with timelines (§164.404 60-day individual notice, §164.408 HHS reporting), required notice content, and the low-probability-of-compromise risk assessment; (3) minimum-necessary policy (§164.502(b)) for PHI accessible to filing personnel; (4) accounting-of-disclosures procedures (§164.528) for filing-related disclosures.
question.notes: Gap detection paired with the sop_compliance question for the same SOP.

output.answer:
SOP-LEGC-005 is **missing a HIPAA-specific breach-notification and de-identification procedure**. It names HIPAA and PHI in scope/definitions, but the operative workflow is generic and only expressly calls out GDPR breach templates; it does not implement the specific HIPAA requirements below.

| Area | Specific missing element | HIPAA requirement |
|---|---|---|
| HIPAA applicability / role determination | No step to determine whether Meridian is acting as a **covered entity** or **business associate** for each filing/reporting event, and therefore whether it must notify individuals/HHS/media directly or notify a covered entity. | HIPAA Part 164 applies to covered entities and, where provided, business associates. 45 CFR § 164.104(a)-(b). Business associates have separate breach-notice duties to covered entities. 45 CFR § 164.410. |
| Breach triage standard | No HIPAA breach-classification workflow for incidents involving **unsecured PHI**, including determining whether a reportable breach has occurred. | A covered entity must notify affected individuals following discovery of a breach of unsecured PHI. 45 CFR § 164.404(a)(1). |
| Discovery trigger | No definition or operational trigger for when a HIPAA breach is “discovered,” including constructive knowledge by workforce members or agents. | A breach is treated as discovered on the first day it is known, or by reasonable diligence would have been known, to the covered entity; knowledge of workforce members or agents is imputed except for the person committing the breach. 45 CFR § 164.404(a)(2). |
| 60-day deadline | No explicit HIPAA deadline requiring individual notice **without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after discovery**. The SOP has a general “zero tolerance for late filing” rule, but not the HIPAA clock. | Individual breach notice must be provided without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery, subject to law-enforcement delay. 45 CFR § 164.404(b); see also § 164.412. |
| Individual notification content | No HIPAA breach-notice template requiring all mandatory content: what happened, breach/discovery dates if known, types of PHI involved, protective steps for individuals, mitigation/investigation/protection actions, and contact procedures. | HIPAA requires those elements in individual breach notices, in plain language. 45 CFR § 164.404(c)(1)-(2). |
| Plain-language requirement | No requirement that HIPAA breach notices be written in **plain language**. | HIPAA requires the individual notice to be written in plain language. 45 CFR § 164.404(c)(2). |
| Individual notice delivery methods | No procedure for first-class mail, electronic notice where the individual agreed and has not withdrawn consent, notice to next of kin/personal representative for deceased individuals, substitute notice, or urgent telephone/other notice. | HIPAA specifies written notice by first-class mail or agreed electronic mail; deceased-individual notice to next of kin/personal representative; substitute notice rules; and additional urgent notice where imminent misuse is possible. 45 CFR § 164.404(d)(1)-(3). |
| Substitute notice thresholds | No rule for substitute notice when contact information is insufficient or outdated, including the different requirements for fewer than 10 individuals versus 10 or more individuals. | For fewer than 10 individuals, substitute notice may be by alternative written notice, telephone, or other means. For 10 or more, substitute notice must be a conspicuous 90-day website posting or major print/broadcast media notice, with a toll-free number active for at least 90 days. 45 CFR § 164.404(d)(2). |
| HHS/OCR notification for 500+ breaches | No requirement to notify the HHS Secretary/OCR for breaches involving **500 or more individuals** contemporaneously with individual notice and via the HHS-specified method. | For breaches involving 500 or more individuals, the covered entity must notify the Secretary contemporaneously with individual notice and in the manner specified on the HHS website. 45 CFR § 164.408(a)-(b). |
| HHS/OCR annual log for <500 breaches | No requirement to maintain a HIPAA breach log for breaches affecting fewer than 500 individuals and submit it to HHS/OCR within 60 days after the end of the calendar year. | For breaches involving fewer than 500 individuals, the covered entity must maintain a log or other documentation and notify the Secretary no later than 60 days after the end of the calendar year. 45 CFR § 164.408(c). |
| Media notice | No trigger or workflow for notifying prominent media outlets when a breach affects more than 500 residents of a state or jurisdiction. | For a breach involving more than 500 residents of a state or jurisdiction, the covered entity must notify prominent media outlets serving that state or jurisdiction without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after discovery; the notice content must meet § 164.404(c). 45 CFR § 164.406(a)-(c). |
| Business associate notification | No business-associate-specific process requiring Meridian, when acting as a BA, to notify the covered entity of a breach, identify affected individuals, and provide information needed for individual notice. | A business associate must notify the covered entity without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after discovery; the notice must identify each affected individual to the extent possible and provide other available information required for individual notices. 45 CFR § 164.410(a)-(c). |
| Law-enforcement delay | No documented process for delaying notices when law enforcement states that notice would impede a criminal investigation or damage national security. | If law enforcement requests delay in writing, notice is delayed for the specified period; if the request is oral, the entity must document the statement and may delay no longer than 30 days unless a written statement is provided. 45 CFR § 164.412. |
| HIPAA burden of proof / documentation | No HIPAA-specific evidence package proving that required notifications were made, or that notification was not required. Generic archival exists, but not HIPAA burden-of-proof documentation. | Covered entities must maintain documentation sufficient to meet their burden of proof regarding breach-notification compliance. 45 CFR § 164.530(j)(1)(iv); see also 45 CFR § 164.414(b). |
| HIPAA retention period | No HIPAA-specific six-year retention requirement for breach-notification documentation, policies, actions, and assessments. | HIPAA documentation must be retained for six years from creation or the date last in effect, whichever is later. 45 CFR § 164.530(j)(2); 45 CFR § 164.316(b)(2)(i). |
| HIPAA security incident linkage | No explicit linkage from security incident response to HIPAA breach reporting. The SOP assigns the Security Incident Response Lead to state breach laws and EU AI Act reporting, but not HIPAA breach reporting. | HIPAA requires entities to identify and respond to security incidents, mitigate harmful effects, and document incidents and outcomes. 45 CFR § 164.308(a)(6)(ii). HIPAA breach notification is then required for breaches of unsecured PHI. 45 CFR § 164.404(a). |
| De-identification governance | No procedure requiring that health information be treated as de-identified only when it does not identify an individual and there is no reasonable basis to believe it can be used to identify an individual. | De-identified health information is information that does not identify an individual and for which there is no reasonable basis to believe it can be used to identify an individual. 45 CFR § 164.514(a). |
| Expert determination method | No expert-determination pathway requiring a qualified statistical/scientific expert to determine that re-identification risk is very small and to document the methods and results. | HIPAA permits de-identification by expert determination only where a person with appropriate statistical/scientific knowledge determines the risk is very small and documents the methods and results. 45 CFR § 164.514(b)(1). |
| Safe Harbor method | No Safe Harbor checklist requiring removal of the 18 categories of identifiers and confirmation that Meridian has no actual knowledge the remaining information could identify an individual. | HIPAA Safe Harbor requires removal of listed identifiers of the individual and relatives, employers, or household members, and requires no actual knowledge that the information could identify the individual. 45 CFR § 164.514(b)(2)(i)-(ii). |
| Safe Harbor identifier list | No required removal list for names, sub-state geography, dates except year, ages over 89, telephone/fax/email, SSNs, MRNs, health plan numbers, account numbers, certificate/license numbers, vehicle/device identifiers, URLs, IP addresses, biometrics, full-face photos, and other unique identifying numbers/characteristics/codes. | These identifiers must be removed under the Safe Harbor method. 45 CFR § 164.514(b)(2)(i)(A)-(R). |
| Re-identification code controls | No rules governing re-identification codes, including prohibiting codes derived from individual information, prohibiting use/disclosure of the code for other purposes, and prohibiting disclosure of the re-identification mechanism. | HIPAA allows a re-identification code only if it is not derived from or related to information about the individual, is not otherwise translatable to identify the individual, is not used or disclosed for other purposes, and the re-identification mechanism is not disclosed. 45 CFR § 164.514(c). |
| Treatment of re-identified data | No rule that if de-identified information is re-identified, it becomes subject to HIPAA use/disclosure rules again. | If de-identified information is re-identified, the covered entity may use or disclose the re-identified information only as permitted or required by HIPAA. 45 CFR § 164.502(d)(2)(ii). |
| Limited data set distinction | No distinction between de-identified data and a **limited data set**, and no process requiring a Data Use Agreement when limited data sets are used in regulatory reporting. | HIPAA limited data sets are still PHI and may be used/disclosed only for research, public health, or health care operations with a compliant data use agreement. 45 CFR § 164.514(e)(1)-(4). |
| Minimum necessary criteria for PHI in filings | No HIPAA-specific rule requiring routine regulatory disclosures of PHI to be limited by standard protocols and non-routine disclosures to be evaluated against criteria designed to limit PHI to the amount reasonably necessary. | HIPAA requires policies/procedures for routine disclosures limiting PHI to the amount reasonably necessary and criteria for non-routine disclosures. 45 CFR § 164.514(d)(3). |

Bottom line: SOP-LEGC-005 has a general regulatory filing framework, but it lacks the HIPAA-specific operational triggers, templates, addressees, deadlines, delivery methods, documentation standards, and de-identification controls required by HIPAA breach-notification and de-identification rules.

**Subpart D—Notification in the Case of Breach of Unsecured Protected Health Information**
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Subpart D—Notification in the Case of Breach of Unsecured Protected Health Information

**164.404 Notification to individuals.**
§ 164.404 Notification to individuals.
  --------------------------------------

(a) Standard—(1) General rule. A covered entity shall, following the discovery of a breach of unsecured protected health information, notify each individual whose unsecured protected health information has been, or is reasonably believed by the covered entity to have been, accessed, acquired, used, or disclosed as a result of such breach.

(2) Breaches treated as discovered. For purposes of paragraph (a)(1) of this section, §§ 164.406(a), and 164.408(a), a breach shall be treated as discovered by a covered entity as of the first day on which such breach is known to the covered entity, or, by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known to the covered entity. A covered entity shall be deemed to have knowledge of a breach if such breach is known, or by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known, to any person, other than the person committing the breach, who is a workforce member or agent of the covered entity (determined in accordance with the federal common law of agency).

(b) Implementation specification: Timeliness of notification. Except as provided in § 164.412, a covered entity shall provide the notification required by paragraph (a) of this section without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of a breach.

(c) Implementation specifications: Content of notification—(1) Elements. The notification required by paragraph (a) of this section shall include, to the extent possible:

(A) A brief description of what happened, including the date of the breach and the date of the discovery of the breach, if known;

(B) A description of the types of unsecured protected health information that were involved in the breach (such as whether full name, social security number, date of birth, home address, account number, diagnosis, disability code, or other types of information were involved);

(C) Any steps individuals should take to protect themselves from potential harm resulting from the breach;

(D) A brief description of what the covered entity involved is doing to investigate the breach, to mitigate harm to individuals, and to protect against any further breaches; and

(E) Contact procedures for individuals to ask questions or learn additional information, which shall include a toll-free telephone number, an e-mail address, Web site, or postal address.

(2) Plain language requirement. The notification required by paragraph (a) of this section shall be written in plain language.

(d) Implementation specifications: Methods of individual notification. The notification required by paragraph (a) of this section shall be provided in the following form:

**PART 164—SECURITY AND PRIVACY**
================================================================================
PART 164—SECURITY AND PRIVACY

**164.408 Notification to the Secretary.**
§ 164.408 Notification to the Secretary.
  ----------------------------------------

    (a) Standard. A covered entity shall, following the discovery of a breach of unsecured protected health information as provided in § 164.404(a)(2), notify the Secretary.

    (b) Implementation specifications: Breaches involving 500 or more individuals. For breaches of unsecured protected health information involving 500 or more individuals, a covered entity shall, except as provided in § 164.412, provide the notification required by paragraph (a) of this section contemporaneously with the notice required by § 164.404(a) and in the manner specified on the HHS Web site.

    (c) Implementation specifications: Breaches involving less than 500 individuals. For breaches of unsecured protected health information involving less than 500 individuals, a covered entity shall maintain a log or other documentation of such breaches and, not later than 60 days after the end of each calendar year, provide the notification required by paragraph (a) of this section for breaches discovered during the preceding calendar year, in the manner specified on the HHS web site.

    [[74 FR 42767, Aug. 24, 2009, as amended at 78 FR 5695, Jan. 25, 2013]]

**164.406 Notification to the media.**
§ 164.406 Notification to the media.
  ------------------------------------

    (a) Standard. For a breach of unsecured protected health information involving more than 500 residents of a State or jurisdiction, a covered entity shall, following the discovery of the breach as provided in § 164.404(a)(2), notify prominent media outlets serving the State or jurisdiction.

    (b) Implementation specification: Timeliness of notification. Except as provided in § 164.412, a covered entity shall provide the notification required by paragraph (a) of this section without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of a breach.

    (c) Implementation specifications: Content of notification. The notification required by paragraph (a) of this section shall meet the requirements of § 164.404(c).

    [[74 FR 42767, Aug. 24, 2009, as amended at 78 FR 5695, Jan. 25, 2013]]

**164.400 Applicability.**
§ 164.400 Applicability.
  ------------------------

    The requirements of this subpart shall apply with respect to breaches of protected health information occurring on or after September 23, 2009.

**164.410 Notification by a business associate.**
§ 164.410 Notification by a business associate.
  -----------------------------------------------

    (a) Standard—(1) General rule. A business associate shall, following the discovery of a breach of unsecured protected health information, notify the covered entity of such breach.

    (2) Breaches treated as discovered. For purposes of paragraph (a)(1) of this section, a breach shall be treated as discovered by a business associate as of the first day on which such breach is known to the business associate or, by exercising reasonable diligence, would have been known to the business associate. A business associate shall be deemed to have knowledge of a breach if the breach is known, or by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known, to any person, other than the person committing the breach, who is an employee, officer, or other agent of the business associate (determined in accordance with the Federal common law of agency).

    (b) Implementation specifications: Timeliness of notification. Except as provided in § 164.412, a business associate shall provide the notification required by paragraph (a) of this section without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of a breach.

    (c) Implementation specifications: Content of notification. (1) The notification required by paragraph (a) of this section shall include, to the extent possible, the identification of each individual whose unsecured protected health information has been, or is reasonably believed by the business associate to have been, accessed, acquired, used, or disclosed during the breach.

    (2) A business associate shall provide the covered entity with any other available information that the covered entity is required to include in notification to the individual under § 164.404(c) at the time of the notification required by paragraph (a) of this section or promptly thereafter as information becomes available.

    [[74 FR 42767, Aug. 24, 2009, as amended at 78 FR 5695, Jan. 25, 2013]]

**164.404 Notification to individuals.**
§ 164.404 Notification to individuals. (continued)

(1) Written notice. (i) Written notification by first-class mail to the individual at the last known address of the individual or, if the individual agrees to electronic notice and such agreement has not been withdrawn, by electronic mail. The notification may be provided in one or more mailings as information is available.

(ii) If the covered entity knows the individual is deceased and has the address of the next of kin or personal representative of the individual (as specified under § 164.502(g)(4) of subpart E), written notification by first-class mail to either the next of kin or personal representative of the individual. The notification may be provided in one or more mailings as information is available.

(2) Substitute notice. In the case in which there is insufficient or out-of-date contact information that precludes written notification to the individual under paragraph (d)(1)(i) of this section, a substitute form of notice reasonably calculated to reach the individual shall be provided. Substitute notice need not be provided in the case in which there is insufficient or out-of-date contact information that precludes written notification to the next of kin or personal representative of the individual under paragraph (d)(1)(ii).

(i) In the case in which there is insufficient or out-of-date contact information for fewer than 10 individuals, then such substitute notice may be provided by an alternative form of written notice, telephone, or other means.

(ii) In the case in which there is insufficient or out-of-date contact information for 10 or more individuals, then such substitute notice shall:

(A) Be in the form of either a conspicuous posting for a period of 90 days on the home page of the Web site of the covered entity involved, or conspicuous notice in major print or broadcast media in geographic areas where the individuals affected by the breach likely reside; and

(B) Include a toll-free phone number that remains active for at least 90 days where an individual can learn whether the individual's unsecured protected health information may be included in the breach.

(3) Additional notice in urgent situations. In any case deemed by the covered entity to require urgency because of possible imminent misuse of unsecured protected health information, the covered entity may provide information to individuals by telephone or other means, as appropriate, in addition to notice provided under paragraph (d)(1) of this section.

**Subpart C—Security Standards for the Protection of Electronic Protected Health Information**
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Subpart C—Security Standards for the Protection of Electronic Protected Health Information

**164.412 Law enforcement delay.**
§ 164.412 Law enforcement delay.
  --------------------------------

    If a law enforcement official states to a covered entity or business associate that a notification, notice, or posting required under this subpart would impede a criminal investigation or cause damage to national security, a covered entity or business associate shall:

    (a) If the statement is in writing and specifies the time for which a delay is required, delay such notification, notice, or posting for the time period specified by the official; or

    (b) If the statement is made orally, document the statement, including the identity of the official making the statement, and delay the notification, notice, or posting temporarily and no longer than 30 days from the date of the oral statement, unless a written statement as described in paragraph (a) of this section is submitted during that time.

**164.514 Other requirements relating to uses and disclosures of protected health information.**
§ 164.514 Other requirements relating to uses and disclosures of protected health information.
  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

(a) Standard: De-identification of protected health information. Health information that does not identify an individual and with respect to which there is no reasonable basis to believe that the information can be used to identify an individual is not individually identifiable health information.

(b) Implementation specifications: Requirements for de-identification of protected health information. A covered entity may determine that health information is not individually identifiable health information only if:

(1) A person with appropriate knowledge of and experience with generally accepted statistical and scientific principles and methods for rendering information not individually identifiable:

(i) Applying such principles and methods, determines that the risk is very small that the information could be used, alone or in combination with other reasonably available information, by an anticipated recipient to identify an individual who is a subject of the information; and

(ii) Documents the methods and results of the analysis that justify such determination; or

(2)(i) The following identifiers of the individual or of relatives, employers, or household members of the individual, are removed:

(A) Names;

(B) All geographic subdivisions smaller than a State, including street address, city, county, precinct, zip code, and their equivalent geocodes, except for the initial three digits of a zip code if, according to the current publicly available data from the Bureau of the Census:

(1) The geographic unit formed by combining all zip codes with the same three initial digits contains more than 20,000 people; and

(2) The initial three digits of a zip code for all such geographic units containing 20,000 or fewer people is changed to 000.

(C) All elements of dates (except year) for dates directly related to an individual, including birth date, admission date, discharge date, date of death; and all ages over 89 and all elements of dates (including year) indicative of such age, except that such ages and elements may be aggregated into a single category of age 90 or older;

§ 164.316 Policies and procedures and documentation requirements.
  -----------------------------------------------------------------

    A covered entity or business associate must, in accordance with § 164.306:

    (a) Standard: Policies and procedures. Implement reasonable and appropriate policies and procedures to comply with the standards, implementation specifications, or other requirements of this subpart, taking into account those factors specified in § 164.306(b)(2)(i), (ii), (iii), and (iv). This standard is not to be construed to permit or excuse an action that violates any other standard, implementation specification, or other requirements of this subpart. A covered entity or business associate may change its policies and procedures at any time, provided that the changes are documented and are implemented in accordance with this subpart.

    (b)(1) Standard: Documentation. (i) Maintain the policies and procedures implemented to comply with this subpart in written (which may be electronic) form; and

    (ii) If an action, activity or assessment is required by this subpart to be documented, maintain a written (which may be electronic) record of the action, activity, or assessment.

    (2) Implementation specifications:

**164.304 Definitions.**
§ 164.304 Definitions.
  ----------------------

As used in this subpart, the following terms have the following meanings:

Access means the ability or the means necessary to read, write, modify, or communicate data/information or otherwise use any system resource. (This definition applies to “access” as used in this subpart, not as used in subparts D or E of this part.)

Administrative safeguards are administrative actions, and policies and procedures, to manage the selection, development, implementation, and maintenance of security measures to protect electronic protected health information and to manage the conduct of the covered entity's or business associate's workforce in relation to the protection of that information.

Authentication means the corroboration that a person is the one claimed.

Availability means the property that data or information is accessible and useable upon demand by an authorized person.

Confidentiality means the property that data or information is not made available or disclosed to unauthorized persons or processes.

Encryption means the use of an algorithmic process to transform data into a form in which there is a low probability of assigning meaning without use of a confidential process or key.

Facility means the physical premises and the interior and exterior of a building(s).

Information system means an interconnected set of information resources under the same direct management control that shares common functionality. A system normally includes hardware, software, information, data, applications, communications, and people.

Integrity means the property that data or information have not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner.

Malicious software means software, for example, a virus, designed to damage or disrupt a system.

Password means confidential authentication information composed of a string of characters.

Physical safeguards are physical measures, policies, and procedures to protect a covered entity's or business associate's electronic information systems and related buildings and equipment, from natural and environmental hazards, and unauthorized intrusion.

Security or Security measures encompass all of the administrative, physical, and technical safeguards in an information system.

Security incident means the attempted or successful unauthorized access, use, disclosure, modification, or destruction of information or interference with system operations in an information system.

Technical safeguards means the technology and the policy and procedures for its use that protect electronic protected health information and control access to it.

User means a person or entity with authorized access.

question.question: Reviewing SOP-AIML-006 (Model Performance Monitoring) against SR 11-7's ongoing monitoring expectations, what specific elements are MISSING?
question.expected_answer: Missing: (1) defined performance thresholds and back-testing cadence tied to model risk tier — monitoring is referenced but specific KPIs and review frequencies are not pinned; (2) challenger-model requirement for high-impact decisions — SR 11-7 expects benchmark/challenger comparisons; (3) escalation path from monitoring findings to senior management and the board (Section V governance); (4) overarching model-risk framework + model inventory anchoring the monitoring activities; (5) explicit linkage between drift signals and re-validation triggers.
