output.answer:
SOP-AIML-006 is strong on automated metric/drift monitoring, alerting, incident response, and reporting, but it is **missing several SR 11-7 ongoing-monitoring elements**.

## Missing elements against SR 11-7 ongoing monitoring

| SR 11-7 expectation | What SOP-AIML-006 has | What is missing |
|---|---|---|
| **Ongoing monitoring should evaluate whether the model continues to perform as expected given changes in products, exposures, activities, clients, data relevance, or market conditions.** SR 11-7, **Section V, Model Validation and Monitoring — Ongoing Model Monitoring**. | SOP monitors data drift, prediction drift, performance drops, latency, traffic, and feature-missing rates. | No explicit monitoring of **business-context changes**: product changes, client/population shifts, new use cases, market/operating-condition changes, or changes in clinical/financial process that could make the model no longer fit for purpose. The SOP treats drift primarily as statistical/technical drift, not as business-use relevance monitoring. |
| **Ongoing monitoring plans may include regular reassessment of model limitations at development and over time, plus procedures for responding to limitation issues.** SR 11-7, **Section V — Ongoing Model Monitoring**. | SOP mentions baselines, metrics, dashboards, and incident RCA. | No recurring **model limitations review**. There is no requirement to re-review documented assumptions, known weaknesses, contraindicated use cases, data limitations, population limitations, or limitations identified during validation. |
| **Validation should identify limitations and errors and clarify appropriate use and whether corrective actions are warranted.** SR 11-7, **Section V, Model Validation and Monitoring**. | SOP has rollback/fallback/feature-off response for critical alerts. | No explicit mechanism to determine whether continued use remains **appropriate** after degradation, drift, delayed-label concerns, or changed use. Escalation is engineering-focused, not a formal “fitness-for-use” or model-risk decision. |
| **When performance deviates meaningfully, organizations should consider adjustment, recalibration, or redevelopment.** SR 11-7, **Section V, Model Validation and Monitoring** and **Ongoing Model Monitoring**. | SOP includes rollback, traffic shunt, feature-off, RCA, and eventual remediation/sunset review after 7 days. | The response playbook does not formally require evaluation of **recalibration**, **model overlays**, **parameter/threshold adjustment**, or **redevelopment** as defined remediation options. “Retraining” appears only parenthetically in Section 8.2, not as a structured remediation path with criteria, approvals, and validation requirements. |
| **Outcomes analysis compares model outputs to real-world outcomes and may include back-testing or outlier analysis.** SR 11-7, **Section V, Components of Model Validation — Outcomes Analysis**. | SOP calculates performance metrics when ground truth is available and uses delayed-label pipelines. | Missing formal **back-testing** and **outlier analysis** procedures. The SOP calculates metrics but does not require periodic analysis of exceptions, tail outcomes, unusually large errors, false positives/false negatives, adverse outcome clusters, or performance under stressed/rare conditions. |
| **Outcomes analysis results should be reviewed for reasonableness and appropriateness, with additional analysis/testing if warranted.** SR 11-7, **Section V — Outcomes Analysis**. | SOP produces dashboards and Model Health Reports. | No required **independent or formally documented review** of outcomes-analysis results for reasonableness. Reports summarize incidents and KPIs, but the SOP does not require a reviewer to challenge whether observed performance remains acceptable for the model’s purpose. |
| **Ongoing monitoring scope and report frequency should depend on model nature, availability of new data/modeling approaches, and model materiality.** SR 11-7, **Section V — Ongoing Model Monitoring**. | SOP has standard windows and weekly/monthly/quarterly reports. | Cadence is mostly fixed and operational. There is no requirement to set monitoring frequency/scope based on **model materiality**, model-risk tier, complexity, use, volatility, data availability, or recent model changes. |
| **Sound validation and monitoring should be commensurate with model use and materiality.** SR 11-7, **Section V, Model Validation and Monitoring**. | SOP distinguishes model categories but applies common monitoring structures. | No explicit **model-risk tiering/materiality mapping** that determines monitoring rigor, thresholds, review frequency, escalation level, independent review depth, or reporting audience. |
| **Model users should understand and communicate limitations, monitor performance, periodically review relevance, and supplement model output with complementary analysis/information.** SR 11-7, **Section V, Model Validation and Monitoring**. | SOP is owned largely by MLOps/Model Owner and includes technical reporting. | No procedure requiring **business/model users** to review relevance, provide feedback, document observed weaknesses, or supplement model outputs when limitations are triggered. User feedback is not part of the monitoring loop. |
| **Using a model beyond its intended purpose introduces additional uncertainty and risk; extensions of use should receive additional analysis of new use and limitations and review of controls.** SR 11-7, **Section IV, Model Use**. | SOP scope includes production, shadow, and A/B testing environments. | No control to detect or approve **use outside intended purpose**. The SOP does not monitor whether production users, products, geographies, patient cohorts, or financial-decision contexts have expanded beyond the approved model use. |
| **Sound model risk management includes effective challenge by objective experts with expertise, independence, and standing to effect change.** SR 11-7, **Section III, Model Risk Management**. | SOP has Model Owner, MLOps, VP Engineering, Director AI/ML, and executives. | Missing **independent model risk / validation review** of ongoing monitoring results, thresholds, exceptions, incidents, and remediation decisions. Accountability sits mainly with development/engineering functions. |
| **Governance should define clear roles and responsibilities across the model lifecycle, including ongoing monitoring, and address conflicts of interest.** SR 11-7, **Section VI, Governance and Controls — Roles and Responsibilities**. | SOP assigns operational roles for MLOps, Model Owner, VP Engineering, etc. | No RACI or accountability for **independent validation**, model risk management, business owner approval, compliance/risk oversight, or conflict-of-interest controls where model owners monitor their own models. |
| **Sound practice includes assessing model risk individually and in aggregate, including dependencies among models and common assumptions, data, or methodologies.** SR 11-7, **Section III, Model Risk Management**. | SOP reports aggregate program KPIs and top models by drift. | Missing **aggregate model-risk monitoring**: shared feature/source failures, correlated model degradation, common vendor/model-family issues, common assumptions, and simultaneous impact across multiple models. |
| **External resources used in model risk management should be properly overseen and integrated into the organization’s model risk management.** SR 11-7, **Section VI, Governance and Controls — Roles and Responsibilities**. | SOP includes third-party/procured models in scope and vendor-hosted SaaS deployment. | No third-party-specific monitoring requirements: contractual access to performance data, vendor monitoring evidence, independent metric verification, service-level reporting, remediation obligations, or integration of vendor results into model risk governance. |
| **Ongoing monitoring may identify persistent deviations outside established thresholds, warranting adjustment, recalibration, or redevelopment.** SR 11-7, **Section V — Outcomes Analysis / Ongoing Model Monitoring**. | SOP has thresholds and a 7-day unresolved-degradation escalation. | Missing criteria for **persistent non-critical degradation** or repeated warning-level breaches. The SOP focuses on Critical alerts; it does not define cumulative-trend triggers, repeated-warning escalation, or chronic underperformance governance. |

## Bottom line

The SOP is **partially aligned** with SR 11-7 because it provides technical monitoring, thresholds, dashboards, incident response, delayed-label performance monitoring, and reporting. However, it is missing SR 11-7’s broader model-risk-management expectations around **business-use relevance, model limitations reassessment, benchmarking/back-testing/outlier analysis, independent effective challenge, materiality-based monitoring scope, user feedback, intended-use monitoring, third-party oversight, and aggregate model-risk monitoring**.

question.question: Reviewing SOP-CLIN-005 (Diagnostic AI Accuracy and Calibration) against NIST AI RMF's MEASURE function (including the GenAI Profile where relevant), what specific elements are MISSING?
question.expected_answer: Missing: (1) bias/fairness/equity testing methodology beyond accuracy — demographic-stratified performance metrics, calibration across protected groups (MEASURE 2/4); (2) AI risk-management framework anchoring measurement to risk tolerance (GOVERN); (3) AI system inventory linking the diagnostic AI to organisational risk (MAP 1); (4) MEASURE coverage of the seven trustworthiness characteristics — safety, security, accountability/transparency, explainability/interpretability, privacy, fair/bias — not just accuracy; (5) post-deployment monitoring closing the loop into MANAGE.

## Bottom line

SOP-CLIN-005 is strong on diagnostic performance, calibration, independent validation, subgroup reporting, drift monitoring, and post-market performance trending. However, against the full NIST AI RMF MEASURE function, it is missing several broader AI risk measurement elements beyond accuracy/calibration. If any diagnostic/CDS product uses generative AI — e.g., LLM-generated clinical summaries, RAG explanations, report drafting, chatbot interfaces, or synthetic data — additional GenAI Profile gaps apply.

## Missing or under-specified elements

| Missing element | Why it is missing from SOP-CLIN-005 | NIST AI RMF basis |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Traceability from mapped AI risks to measurement methods** | The SOP defines clinical performance metrics and calibration gates, but it does not require a measurement plan that traces each metric to AI risks identified during the MAP function, nor does it require documentation of risks that cannot or will not be measured. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 1.1 requires measurement approaches and metrics to be selected for AI risks enumerated during MAP, starting with the most significant risks, and requires documentation of risks that cannot or will not be measured. |
| **2. Periodic reassessment of whether metrics and controls remain appropriate** | The SOP monitors model metrics monthly and quarterly, but it does not require periodic review of whether the chosen metrics, thresholds, and controls are still valid or effective, including in light of error reports and potential impacts on affected communities. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 1.2 requires the appropriateness of AI metrics and effectiveness of controls to be regularly assessed and updated, including reports of errors and potential impacts on affected communities. |
| **3. Consultation with affected communities and end users in measurement updates** | The SOP uses a Clinical Validation Lead and Medical Advisory Board, but it does not establish structured consultation with affected patients, patient advocates, frontline clinicians as end users, or other impacted communities for measurement design and updates. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 1.3 calls for internal experts and/or independent assessors, and consultation with domain experts, users, external AI actors, and affected communities as necessary. MEASURE 4.1–4.3 also require measurement approaches and results to be informed by domain experts, end users, relevant AI actors, affected communities, and field data. |
| **4. Full TEVV tool documentation** | The SOP identifies some tooling, such as MLflow/LangSmith, but does not require complete documentation of TEVV tools, versions, configurations, validation status, evaluation environment, or reproducibility parameters. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.1 requires test sets, metrics, and details about tools used during TEVV to be documented. |
| **5. Human-subject protection requirements for clinical evaluations** | The SOP requires independent clinical validation and chart review, but it does not explicitly require IRB/ethics review, informed consent or waiver determinations, human-subject protection documentation, or equivalent applicable clinical research compliance determinations. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.2 requires evaluations involving human subjects to meet applicable requirements, including human-subject protection, and to be representative of the relevant population. |
| **6. Formal documentation of generalizability limits** | The SOP requires an independent validation dataset and subgroup analysis, but it does not require a formal “limitations of generalizability” section documenting where the model should not be assumed valid, such as new sites, devices, protocols, disease prevalence shifts, pediatric/geriatric populations, rare conditions, or non-represented subgroups. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.5 requires the deployed AI system to be demonstrated valid and reliable and requires limitations of generalizability beyond development conditions to be documented. |
| **7. Residual safety-risk measurement and fail-safe criteria** | The SOP has low-confidence suppression, input validation, and incident handling, but it does not define measurable safety-risk criteria tied to organizational risk tolerance, residual negative risk acceptance, robustness under out-of-distribution conditions, or safe failure when operating beyond knowledge limits. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.6 requires regular evaluation of safety risks, demonstration that residual negative risk does not exceed risk tolerance, and evidence that the system can fail safely, especially beyond knowledge limits. |
| **8. Documented security and resilience evaluation** | The SOP includes an adversarial input filter, access controls, and audit logs, but it does not require a documented security/resilience test program covering model extraction, membership inference, data poisoning, adversarial examples, dependency compromise, model theft, or penetration testing. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.7 requires AI system security and resilience risks to be evaluated and documented. For GenAI, NIST AI 600-1 MS-2.7-001 calls for assessing threats such as backdoors, compromised dependencies, data breaches, reverse engineering, model theft or exposure of weights, inference, bypass, and extraction; MS-2.7-007 calls for AI red-teaming against prompt injection, adversarial prompts, data poisoning, membership inference, model extraction, and related attacks. |
| **9. Transparency and accountability risk assessment** | The SOP requires confidence scores and audit logs, but it does not require a formal assessment of transparency and accountability risks, such as whether clinicians understand model uncertainty, whether explanations induce overreliance, whether audit logs support accountability, or whether accountability gaps exist between vendor, clinician, and health system. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.8 requires risks associated with transparency and accountability to be examined and documented. |
| **10. Validated explainability and contextual interpretation** | The SOP requires confidence scores in natural language or visual formats, but it does not require validated explanation methods, evaluation of explanation fidelity, explanation limitations, or evidence that outputs are interpreted appropriately in clinical context. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.9 requires the AI model to be explained, validated, and documented, and requires AI system output to be interpreted within context. For GenAI, NIST AI 600-1 MS-2.9-001 calls for documenting ML explanation results such as embedding analysis, counterfactual prompts, gradient-based attributions, surrogate models, or occlusion/term reduction; MS-2.9-002 calls for documenting model details including assumptions, limitations, data provenance, architecture, optimization objectives, training algorithms, RLHF, fine-tuning, RAG, evaluation data, ethical considerations, and legal/regulatory requirements. |
| **11. Privacy-risk measurement and documentation** | The SOP mentions HIPAA-compliant logs, but it does not require a privacy risk assessment of model inputs, outputs, logs, training/validation data, re-identification risk, membership inference risk, or leakage of sensitive health information. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.10 requires privacy risk of the AI system to be examined and documented. For GenAI, NIST AI 600-1 MS-2.10-001 calls for AI red-teaming for outputting training data samples, reverse engineering, model extraction, membership inference, and revealing biometric, confidential, copyrighted, licensed, personal, proprietary, sensitive, or trade-marked information. |
| **12. Bias-source measurement beyond performance disparities** | The SOP requires subgroup performance reporting, but it does not require measurement of bias sources in training and TEVV data, intersectional subgroup coverage, proxy variables, representativeness gaps, label bias, digital divide effects, or bias introduced by synthetic/GAI-generated data. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.11 requires fairness and bias to be evaluated and documented. For GenAI, NIST AI 600-1 MS-2.11-004 calls for reviewing, documenting, and measuring sources of bias in training and TEVV data, including subgroup coverage, proxy features, representativeness, and prevalence of GAI-generated data; MS-2.11-005 calls for assessing the proportion of synthetic to non-synthetic training data to mitigate model-collapse concerns. |
| **13. Environmental impact and sustainability measurement** | The SOP does not address energy use, compute intensity, water consumption, carbon impact, or sustainability tradeoffs for model training, fine-tuning, deployment, or monitoring. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.12 requires environmental impact and sustainability of AI model training and management activities to be assessed and documented. For GenAI, NIST AI 600-1 MS-2.12-002 requires documenting anticipated environmental impacts in product design decisions, and MS-2.12-003 calls for measuring or estimating energy and water consumption for training, fine-tuning, and deployment. |
| **14. Evaluation of the measurement process itself** | The SOP defines performance and calibration metrics, but it does not require periodic evaluation of whether the TEVV process and selected metrics are effective, construct-valid, reproducible, or biased. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.13 requires the effectiveness of TEVV metrics and processes to be evaluated and documented. For GenAI, NIST AI 600-1 MS-2.13-001 calls for measurement error models for pre-deployment metrics, including bias or statistical variance in metrics and structured human feedback processes. |
| **15. Tracking of unanticipated and emergent AI risks** | The SOP tracks drift, latency, errors, low-confidence rates, calibration, and adverse events, but it does not establish a process to identify and track unanticipated or emergent AI risks that were not part of the original validation protocol. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 3.1 requires approaches, personnel, and documentation to regularly identify and track existing, unanticipated, and emergent AI risks based on intended and actual performance in deployed contexts. For GenAI, NIST AI 600-1 MS-3.2-001 calls for processes to identify emergent GAI risks, including consultation with external AI actors. |
| **16. Approach for risks that are hard to measure or lack metrics** | The SOP does not define fallback measurement approaches for risks where metrics are immature or unavailable, such as clinician overreliance, automation bias, rare subgroup harms, long-term outcome harms, or sociotechnical impacts. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 3.2 requires risk tracking approaches to be considered where AI risks are difficult to assess using currently available measurement techniques or where metrics are not yet available. |
| **17. User and impacted-community reporting and appeal mechanisms integrated into metrics** | The SOP includes clinician AI concordance fields and adverse-event summaries, but it does not create a formal feedback and appeal process for end users or impacted patients/communities, nor does it integrate such reports into evaluation metrics. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 3.3 requires feedback processes for end users and impacted communities to report problems and appeal system outcomes and requires those processes to be integrated into AI system evaluation metrics. |
| **18. Field-data feedback on measurement efficacy** | The SOP’s QBR is internally focused and does not require documented assessment of whether field data and stakeholder feedback show performance improvements or declines in context-relevant trustworthiness characteristics. | NIST AI RMF MEASURE 4.2 requires measurement results across deployment contexts and the AI lifecycle to be informed by domain experts and relevant AI actors, and MEASURE 4.3 requires measurable performance improvements or declines based on consultations with relevant AI actors, affected communities, and field data to be identified and documented. |

## Additional GenAI-specific missing elements, if the diagnostic AI includes GAI functionality

These are conditional gaps: they matter if the product uses LLMs, RAG, generated reports, generated explanations, synthetic data, or conversational interfaces.

| GenAI-specific missing element | Why it is missing | NIST GenAI Profile basis |
|---|---|---|
| **Confabulation / hallucination measurement** | The SOP does not define metrics or tests for generated clinical text that may be confidently false, internally inconsistent, or unsupported by the patient record. | NIST AI 600-1 §2.2 defines confabulation as confidently stated erroneous or false content and specifically notes healthcare risks such as confabulated patient summaries causing incorrect diagnoses or treatments. |
| **Citation/source verification for generated outputs** | The SOP does not require source/citation verification for generated clinical summaries, explanations, or recommendations. | NIST AI 600-1 MS-2.5-003 calls for reviewing and verifying sources and citations in GAI outputs during pre-deployment risk measurement and ongoing monitoring. |
| **RAG/fine-tuning data groundedness and provenance** | The SOP addresses clinical ground truth for diagnostic labels, but it does not require provenance verification for RAG corpora, fine-tuning data, or generated/synthetic training data. | NIST AI 600-1 MS-2.5-005 requires verification of GAI training and TEVV data provenance and verification that fine-tuning or RAG data is grounded. |
| **Synthetic-data controls** | The SOP does not require deduplication checks or measurement of the proportion of synthetic to non-synthetic data. | NIST AI 600-1 MS-2.10-003 calls for verifying deduplication of GAI training data samples, particularly synthetic data; MS-2.11-005 calls for assessing the proportion of synthetic to non-synthetic training data. |
| **Content provenance and authentication** | The SOP does not require watermarking, cryptographic signatures, digital fingerprints, provenance metadata, or measurement of false positives/false negatives for generated content authentication. | NIST AI 600-1 MS-2.7-002 calls for benchmarking GAI security and resilience related to content provenance; MS-2.7-005 calls for measuring reliability of content authentication methods, including watermarking, cryptographic signatures, digital fingerprints, and false positive/false negative rates. Appendix A.1.6 describes provenance metadata, watermarking, metadata recording, and digital fingerprinting for tracing content origins and modifications. |
| **Prompt-injection and jailbreak red-teaming** | The SOP has an adversarial input filter for anomalous inputs, but it does not require GAI red-teaming for prompt injection, jailbreaks, harmful outputs, model extraction, or privacy leakage. | NIST AI 600-1 MS-2.7-007 calls for AI red-teaming against prompt injection, adversarial prompts, data poisoning, membership inference, model extraction, and related attacks. |
| **Anthropomorphization and overreliance tracking** | The SOP evaluates human factors generally, but it does not require tracking anthropomorphic interface cues or user perception of generated content/provenance. | NIST AI 600-1 MS-2.5-004 calls for tracking anthropomorphization in GAI interfaces; MS-3.3-002 calls for studies on how end users perceive and interact with GAI content and provenance in context of use. |
| **GAI-specific model documentation** | The SOP release package does not require GenAI model documentation covering architecture, optimization objectives, RLHF, fine-tuning, RAG, evaluation data, assumptions, limitations, ethical considerations, and legal/regulatory requirements. | NIST AI 600-1 MS-2.9-002 calls for documenting these GAI model details. |

Value Chain and Component Integration GAI value chains involve many third-party components such as procured datasets, pre-trained models, and software libraries. These components might be improperly obtained or not properly vetted, leading to diminished transparency or accountability for downstream users. While this is a risk for traditional AI systems and some other digital technologies, the risk is exacerbated for GAI due to the scale of the training data, which may be too large for humans to vet; the diﬃculty of training foundation models, which leads to extensive reuse of limited numbers of models; and the extent to which GAI may be integrated into other devices and services. NIST AI 100-1 AI RMF 1.0 When applying the AI RMF, risks which the organization determines to be highest for the AI systems within a given context of use call for the most urgent prioritization and most thorough risk management process. In cases where an AI system presents unacceptable negative risk levels – such as where significant negative impacts are imminent, severe harms are actually occurring, or catastrophic risks are present – development and deployment should cease in a safe manner until risks can be sufficiently managed. If an AI system’s development, deployment, and use cases are found to be low-risk in a specific context, that may suggest potentially lower prioritization. Risk prioritization may differ between AI systems that are designed or deployed to directly interact with humans as compared to AI systems that are not. Higher initial prioritization may be called for in settings where the AI system is trained on large datasets comprised of sensitive or protected data such as personally identifiable information, or where the outputs of the AI systems have direct or indirect impact on humans. AI systems designed to interact only with computational systems and trained on non-sensitive datasets (for example, data collected from the physical environment) may call for lower initial prioritization. Nonethe- less, regularly assessing and prioritizing risk based on context remains important because non-human-facing AI systems can have downstream safety or social implications. Residual risk – defined as risk remaining after risk treatment (Source: ISO GUIDE 73) – directly impacts end users or affected individuals and communities. Documenting residual risks will call for the system provider to fully consider the risks of deploying the AI product and will inform end users about potential negative impacts of interacting with the system. 1.2.4 Organizational Integration and Management of Risk AI risks should not be considered in isolation. 6 2.2. Confabulation “Confabulation” refers to a phenomenon in which GAI systems generate and conﬁdently present erroneous or false content in response to prompts. Confabulations also include generated outputs that diverge from the prompts or other input or that contradict previously generated statements in the same context. These phenomena are colloquially also referred to as “hallucinations” or “fabrications.” Confabulations can occur across GAI outputs and contexts.9,10 Confabulations are a natural result of the way generative models are designed: they generate outputs that approximate the statistical distribution of their training data; for example, LLMs predict the next token or word in a sentence or phrase. While such statistical prediction can produce factually accurate and consistent outputs, it can also produce outputs that are factually inaccurate or internally inconsistent. This dynamic is particularly relevant when it comes to open-ended prompts for long-form responses and in domains which require highly contextual and/or domain expertise. Risks from confabulations may arise when users believe false content – often due to the conﬁdent nature of the response – leading users to act upon or promote the false information. This poses a challenge for many real-world applications, such as in healthcare, where a confabulated summary of patient information reports could cause doctors to make incorrect diagnoses and/or recommend the wrong treatments. Risks of confabulated content may be especially important to monitor when integrating GAI into applications involving consequential decision making. GAI outputs may also include confabulated logic or citations that purport to justify or explain the system’s answer, which may further mislead humans into inappropriately trusting the system’s output. For instance, LLMs sometimes provide logical steps for how they arrived at an answer even when the answer itself is incorrect. Similarly, an LLM could falsely assert that it is human or has human traits, potentially deceiving humans into believing they are speaking with another human. The extent to which humans can be deceived by LLMs, the mechanisms by which this may occur, and the potential risks from adversarial prompting of such behavior are emerging areas of study. Given the wide range of downstream impacts of GAI, it is diﬃcult to estimate the downstream scale and impact of confabulations. Environmental Impacts Training, maintaining, and operating (running inference on) GAI systems are resource-intensive activities, with potentially large energy and environmental footprints. Energy and carbon emissions vary based on what is being done with the GAI model (i.e., pre-training, ﬁne-tuning, inference), the modality of the content, hardware used, and type of task or application. Current estimates suggest that training a single transformer LLM can emit as much carbon as 300 round- trip ﬂights between San Francisco and New York. In a study comparing energy consumption and carbon emissions for LLM inference, generative tasks (e.g., text summarization) were found to be more energy- and carbon-i ntensive th an discriminative or non-generative tasks (e.g., text classiﬁcation). Methods for creating smaller versions of trained models, such as model distillation or compression, could reduce environmental impacts at inference time, but training and tuning such models may still contribute to their environmental impacts. Currently there is no agreed upon method to estimate environmental impacts from GAI. Trustworthy AI Characteristics: Accountable and Transparent, Safe 2.6. NIST AI 100-1 AI RMF 1.0 Social responsibility can refer to the organization’s responsibility “for the impacts of its decisions and activities on society and the environment through transparent and ethical behavior” ( ISO 26000:2010). Sustainability refers to the “state of the global system, including environmental, social, and economic aspects, in which the needs of the present are met without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs” ( ISO /IEC TR 24368:2022). Responsible AI is meant to result in technology that is also equitable and accountable. The expectation is that organizational practices are carried out in accord with “professional responsibility,” defined by ISO as an approach that “aims to ensure that professionals who design, develop, or deploy AI systems and applications or AI-based products or systems, recognize their unique position to exert influence on people, society, and the future of AI” (ISO /IEC TR 24368:2022). The Framework is intended to be voluntary, rights-preserving, non-sector-specific, and use-case agnostic, providing flexibil- ity to organizations of all sizes and in all sectors and throughout society to implement the approaches in the Framework. question.question: Reviewing SOP-AIML-009 (Algorithmic Bias Detection and Mitigation) against GDPR Article 35 (DPIA) and Article 22 (automated decision-making), what specific procedures are MISSING?
question.expected_answer: Missing: (1) Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) procedure under Article 35 — systematic description of processing, necessity/proportionality assessment, risks-to-rights evaluation, measures envisaged; (2) prior-consultation procedure with the supervisory authority (Article 36) when residual risk remains high; (3) Article 22 procedures for solely-automated significant-effect decisions — meaningful information about the logic involved, right to obtain human intervention, right to express the data subject's point of view, right to contest the decision; (4) Articles 13/14 specificity in privacy notices regarding the bias-detection processing and its purposes.
question.notes: Gap detection across multiple GDPR articles for a bias SOP.

output.answer:
Below are the **specific missing procedures** in SOP-AIML-009 when reviewed against **GDPR Article 35 — DPIA** and **GDPR Article 22 — automated individual decision-making**.

| Area | Missing procedure | Why it is missing / regulatory basis |
|---|---|---|
| **DPIA trigger determination** | A mandatory **DPIA screening/trigger procedure** for every AI/ML use case before development or deployment, including whether the system involves systematic and extensive evaluation/profiling producing legal or similarly significant effects, or large-scale special category data processing. | GDPR requires a DPIA before processing likely to result in high risk, especially using new technologies, and specifically identifies systematic extensive automated evaluation/profiling and large-scale special category data processing as DPIA-triggering cases. **GDPR Art. 35(1), 35(3)(a), 35(3)(b).** SOP-AIML-009 only requires a privacy consultation ticket when bias testing involves PII/PHI, not a full DPIA trigger assessment for the AI/ML processing itself. **SOP 5.1.5.** |
| **Formal DPIA completion gate** | A deployment gate requiring a **completed and approved DPIA before processing/deployment** for in-scope high-risk AI/ML systems. | GDPR requires the controller to carry out the DPIA **prior to processing** where high risk is likely. **GDPR Art. 35(1).** SOP-AIML-009 gates deployment on bias governance artifacts, model cards, fairness assessments, and privacy consultation ticket approval where required, but not on DPIA completion/approval. **SOP 5.4.2–5.4.3.** |
| **DPIA content checklist** | A required DPIA template/checklist covering: systematic description of processing and purposes; legitimate interest where applicable; necessity and proportionality; risks to data subjects’ rights and freedoms; and measures/safeguards/security mechanisms to address risks and demonstrate GDPR compliance. | GDPR specifies these minimum DPIA contents. **GDPR Art. 35(7)(a)–(d).** SOP-AIML-009 has a Bias Testing Plan and Model Card, but these focus on fairness metrics, protected attributes, proxy detection, model performance, and remediation—not the full GDPR DPIA content set. **SOP 5.1, 5.4.1.** |
| **DPO advice during DPIA** | A procedure requiring the project team/controller to **seek DPO advice when carrying out the DPIA**, with evidence of advice received and disposition of recommendations. | GDPR requires the controller to seek the advice of the DPO, where designated, when carrying out a DPIA. **GDPR Art. 35(2).** SOP-AIML-009 requires consulting the EU DPO for PII/PHI used in bias testing and says the DPO reviews DPIAs where algorithmic bias creates high risk, but it does not require DPO advice for all Article 35-triggered DPIAs. **SOP 3; SOP 5.1.5.** |
| **Data subject / representative consultation** | A procedure to determine when it is appropriate to **seek the views of data subjects or their representatives** on the intended AI/ML processing, and to document the outcome or rationale for not doing so. | GDPR requires controllers, where appropriate, to seek the views of data subjects or their representatives on intended processing, subject to protections for commercial/public interests or security. **GDPR Art. 35(9).** SOP-AIML-009 has internal consultation with Product, Compliance, Legal, IRB, and the DPO, but no external/data-subject consultation process. **SOP 3; SOP 5.1; SOP 5.4.3.** |
| **DPIA review/update on risk change** | A procedure requiring DPIA review when model changes, data changes, use-case changes, drift, new populations, new protected-attribute proxies, or monitoring results change the risk profile. | GDPR requires review where necessary to assess whether processing is performed in accordance with the DPIA, at least when there is a change of the risk represented by processing operations. **GDPR Art. 35(11).** SOP-AIML-009 has fairness re-validation and bias drift monitoring, but it does not link those events to DPIA review/update. **SOP 5.6.2–5.6.3.** |
| **Supervisory authority DPIA-list check** | A procedure to check applicable EU/Member State supervisory authority lists of processing operations that require or do not require a DPIA. | Supervisory authorities publish lists of processing operations subject to DPIA requirements and may publish lists where no DPIA is required. **GDPR Art. 35(4)–(5).** SOP-AIML-009 does not include a country-specific DPIA-list check despite operating in the EU, including London/Berlin scope. **SOP 1.2.** |
| **Consideration of approved codes of conduct** | A procedure to consider applicable approved codes of conduct when assessing processing impacts and safeguards. | GDPR requires compliance with approved codes of conduct to be taken into account in DPIAs where relevant. **GDPR Art. 35(8).** SOP-AIML-009 references NIST SP 1270 and ISO/IEC 42001, but not GDPR-approved codes of conduct as a DPIA input. **SOP 10.2.** |
| **Residual high-risk escalation / prior consultation handoff** | A procedure requiring escalation to the privacy/legal team and, where required, supervisory authority prior consultation if the DPIA shows residual high risk after mitigation. | Where a DPIA indicates high risk in the absence of measures taken by the controller to mitigate the risk, the controller must consult the supervisory authority before processing. **GDPR Art. 36(1).** SOP-AIML-009 has internal exception handling and escalation for bias issues, but no supervisory-authority consultation trigger or handoff from DPIA outcomes. **SOP 8.2–8.3.** |
| **Article 22 applicability assessment** | A procedure to classify each model/use case as involving or not involving a **solely automated decision** that produces legal or similarly significant effects. | GDPR gives data subjects the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produce legal or similarly significant effects. **GDPR Art. 22(1).** SOP-AIML-009 prohibits fully automated consequential decisions only for Critical/High-risk models, but it does not create an Article 22 legal/significant-effects assessment for all models, including Standard/Low models. **SOP 4.3.** |
| **Article 22 legal basis / exception check** | A procedure requiring documentation that any solely automated legal/significant decision is permitted only because it is necessary for contract, authorized by Union/Member State law with safeguards, or based on explicit consent. | GDPR permits Article 22 decisions only under these exceptions. **GDPR Art. 22(2)(a)–(c).** SOP-AIML-009 does not require project teams to document which Article 22 exception applies before using solely automated decision-making. **SOP 5.1; SOP 5.4.** |
| **Data subject right to human intervention** | A customer/data-subject-facing procedure for individuals to request **human intervention** after an automated decision. | For Article 22 decisions based on contract necessity or explicit consent, GDPR requires safeguards including the right to obtain human intervention. **GDPR Art. 22(3).** SOP-AIML-009 requires meaningful human oversight for High/Critical consequential decisions, but that is an internal operating control and does not define a data-subject request process. **SOP 4.3.** |
| **Right to express point of view** | A procedure allowing affected individuals to submit their point of view, evidence, or contextual information before or after an automated decision is finalized/reviewed. | GDPR requires safeguards including the right for the data subject to express their point of view. **GDPR Art. 22(3).** SOP-AIML-009 has no intake, review, or documentation mechanism for receiving a data subject’s point of view. **SOP 4.3; SOP 8.3.** |
| **Right to contest automated decision** | A procedure for individuals to **contest the decision**, including intake channel, identity verification, reviewer assignment, re-assessment steps, outcome communication, and recordkeeping. | GDPR requires safeguards including the right to contest the decision. **GDPR Art. 22(3).** SOP-AIML-009 covers internal bias incidents and exceptions, but not individual contestation of an automated decision. **SOP 8.2–8.3.** |
| **Special category data restriction for Article 22 decisions** | A procedure prohibiting Article 22 automated decisions based on special category data unless the Article 22(4) conditions are met, and requiring documentation of the applicable Article 9 basis and safeguards. | GDPR prohibits Article 22 decisions based on special categories of personal data unless Article 9(2)(a) or 9(2)(g) applies and suitable safeguards are in place. **GDPR Art. 22(4).** SOP-AIML-009 addresses PII/PHI minimization for bias testing, but not the separate Article 22 restriction on automated decisions using special category data. **SOP 4.4; SOP 5.1.5.** |
| **Transparency notice linkage for automated decisions** | A procedure requiring privacy notices to disclose the existence of Article 22 automated decision-making/profiling, meaningful information about the logic involved, and significance/envisaged consequences. | GDPR requires this information where personal data are collected from the data subject and Article 22 automated decision-making/profiling exists. **GDPR Art. 13(2)(f).** SOP-AIML-009 requires Model Cards, but Model Cards are internal ML registry documents and are not a data-subject notice process. **SOP 4.5; SOP 5.4.1.** |

**Bottom line:** SOP-AIML-009 is strong on technical bias testing, fairness metrics, remediation, model-card documentation, and internal human oversight. However, it is missing the GDPR-specific procedural layer for **DPIA governance** and **data-subject rights around automated decisions**. The biggest gaps are: no mandatory Article 35 DPIA trigger/completion gate, no full DPIA content workflow, no data-subject consultation process, no DPIA refresh trigger, no Article 22 legal-basis/exception assessment, and no operational process for individuals to obtain human intervention, express their view, or contest automated decisions.

question.question: Reviewing SOP-PENG-001 (Secure Software Development Lifecycle) against EU AI Act Article 9 (risk management system), what specific elements are MISSING for an SDLC supporting high-risk AI systems?
question.expected_answer: Missing: (1) continuous lifecycle risk-management process (Article 9 §2) — identification/analysis/estimation/evaluation of risks throughout development and after deployment, integrated into the SDLC phases; (2) elimination or reduction of identified risks through design and development decisions (Article 9 §4); (3) testing procedures explicitly verifying high-risk AI requirements against acceptable residual risk thresholds (Article 9 §6, §7); (4) consideration of foreseeable misuse and the use environment in risk assessment (Article 9 §3); (5) linkage to post-market-monitoring data feeding back into the SDLC (Article 9 §2 lifecycle loop).

output.answer:
SOP-PENG-001 has a solid **secure SDLC** foundation, but it is **not sufficient as an EU AI Act Article 9 risk management system** for high-risk AI systems. The missing elements are below.

## Specific Article 9 elements missing

| Missing element | Why it is missing / insufficient | EU AI Act basis |
|---|---|---|
| **1. A formal high-risk AI risk management system distinct from general SSDLC/security risk management** | SOP-PENG-001 establishes a security-focused SSDLC and threat modeling process, but it does not establish, implement, document, and maintain a dedicated **risk management system for each high-risk AI system**. Its “High” impact rating is security-oriented and includes “AI/ML model serving endpoint publicly exposed,” but it does not classify or manage systems as **EU AI Act high-risk AI systems**. | Article 9(1) requires a risk management system to be “established, implemented, documented and maintained” for high-risk AI systems. |
| **2. Lifecycle-wide, iterative AI risk review and update process** | The SOP has annual threat modeling for Tier-1 applications and post-deployment vulnerability monitoring, but it does not require regular systematic AI risk reviews across the entire AI lifecycle, including model retraining, performance drift, new use contexts, new affected populations, or changed intended purpose. | Article 9(2) requires the system to be a “continuous iterative process” throughout the entire lifecycle, with regular systematic review and updating. |
| **3. Explicit identification and analysis of risks to health, safety, and fundamental rights** | The SOP focuses on cybersecurity, ePHI, privacy, access control, audit logs, encryption, STRIDE threats, and abuse stories. It does not require identification of AI risks to **health**, **safety**, or **fundamental rights**, such as discriminatory outcomes, denial of services, clinical harm, automation bias, loss of human agency, or unjustified differential treatment. | Article 9(2)(a) requires identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights. |
| **4. Intended-purpose and reasonably foreseeable misuse analysis for AI-specific harms** | SOP-PENG-001 includes STRIDE threat modeling and attacker “abuser stories,” but it does not require evaluation of risks arising from use according to the AI system’s intended purpose or from reasonably foreseeable misuse by deployers or users, such as off-label clinical use, overreliance on model outputs, inappropriate use on unsupported populations, or use with poor-quality input data. | Article 9(2)(b) requires estimating and evaluating risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse. |
| **5. Post-market monitoring feedback loop into the risk management system** | The SOP’s Operations phase covers vulnerability scanning, dependency monitoring, CVE remediation, CSPM alerts, and bug bounty intake, but it does not require systematic collection and analysis of post-market AI performance, incidents, user/deployer feedback, drift, bias signals, near misses, or complaints to update the AI risk assessment. | Article 9(2)(c) requires evaluation of other risks based on data gathered from the post-market monitoring system referred to in Article 72. Article 72(1)-(3) requires providers to establish and document a post-market monitoring system and plan that actively and systematically collects, documents, and analyses relevant performance data throughout the AI system’s lifetime. |
| **6. Targeted AI risk-control measures tied to each identified risk** | The SOP requires security mitigations in the Threat Model Document, but it does not require AI-specific controls mapped to each health, safety, and fundamental-rights hazard, such as bias mitigation, guardrails, human review thresholds, override mechanisms, input-quality checks, monitoring thresholds, escalation workflows, or restrictions on use. | Article 9(2)(d) requires appropriate and targeted risk management measures for identified risks. |
| **7. Residual-risk acceptability criteria for each hazard and for the overall AI system** | The SOP’s threat model includes inherent risk, mitigations, and residual risk, but it does not define EU AI Act-style criteria for when residual risk is acceptable for **each hazard** and for the **overall high-risk AI system**. It also lacks a formal sign-off standard for AI residual risk before placing on the market or putting into service. | Article 9(5) requires the residual risk associated with each hazard, and the overall residual risk of the high-risk AI system, to be judged acceptable. |
| **8. Risk-control hierarchy: design-out risks first, then mitigation/control measures, then deployer information/training** | SOP-PENG-001 has security-by-design principles, but it does not require a documented hierarchy showing that AI risks were eliminated or reduced through design where technically feasible before relying on downstream controls, warnings, training, or instructions. | Article 9(5)(a)-(c) requires risk elimination or reduction through design and development where technically feasible, mitigation/control measures for risks that cannot be eliminated, and provision of Article 13 information and, where appropriate, training to deployers. |
| **9. Consideration of interactions among all high-risk AI requirements** | The SOP maps to HIPAA and SOC 2 controls and includes security, privacy, and vulnerability management, but it does not require analysis of how AI Act requirements interact—for example, how data governance, logging, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity controls may affect one another and the overall risk profile. | Article 9(4) requires risk management measures to consider the effects and possible interaction from the combined application of the requirements in Chapter III, Section 2. |
| **10. AI testing to identify risk management measures** | SOP testing is security-focused: QA security tests, DAST, penetration testing, vulnerability scanning, and CI gates. It does not require AI risk testing to identify the most appropriate risk controls, such as model validation against safety metrics, subgroup performance, bias/fairness testing, robustness testing, calibration, false positive/false negative impact analysis, or human-oversight effectiveness testing. | Article 9(6) requires high-risk AI systems to be tested to identify the most appropriate and targeted risk management measures and to ensure consistent performance for the intended purpose and compliance with Section 2 requirements. |
| **11. Prior-defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds for AI testing** | The SOP defines security gates such as zero Critical/High SAST findings, DAST blockers, and CVE SLAs, but it does not define AI performance metrics or probabilistic thresholds before testing, such as sensitivity/specificity, false negative thresholds, subgroup error-rate limits, confidence thresholds, drift thresholds, or safety escalation thresholds. | Article 9(8) requires testing to be performed against prior-defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds appropriate to the intended purpose. |
| **12. Testing before placing on the market or putting into service, plus appropriate testing during development** | The SOP requires security testing before release, but it does not expressly require high-risk AI conformity-oriented testing before placing the AI system on the EU market or putting it into service, nor does it require AI testing “at any time throughout the development process” as appropriate. | Article 9(8) requires testing, as appropriate, throughout development and in any event before placing on the market or putting into service. |
| **13. Decision process for real-world testing** | Article 9 does not require real-world testing in every case, but the SOP lacks criteria for when real-world testing is needed for high-risk AI risk controls and how such testing would be governed. | Article 9(7) states testing procedures may include testing in real-world conditions in accordance with Article 60. |
| **14. Deployer context, deployer competence, and expected training considered in risk controls** | SOP-PENG-001 has internal role-based training for Meridian personnel, but it does not require the AI risk assessment to consider the deployer’s expected technical knowledge, experience, education, training, or the context in which the system will be used. | Article 9 continuation after Article 9(5) requires due consideration of the deployer’s technical knowledge, experience, education, expected training, and presumable use context. |
| **15. Article 13 deployer information package linked to risk management** | The SOP does not require instructions for use for deployers containing the intended purpose, performance characteristics, limitations, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity metrics, known foreseeable risks, human oversight measures, input-data specifications, or information needed to interpret outputs. | Article 9(5)(c) requires provision of information required under Article 13. Article 13(2)-(3) requires concise, complete, correct, clear, accessible, and comprehensible instructions for use, including intended purpose, performance limitations, foreseeable risk circumstances, human oversight measures, and input-data specifications. |
| **16. Assessment of impacts on persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups** | The SOP does not require a specific analysis of whether a high-risk AI system is likely to adversely affect minors or other vulnerable groups. | Article 9(9) requires providers to consider whether, in view of the intended purpose, the high-risk AI system is likely to adversely affect persons under 18 or other vulnerable groups. |
| **17. AI-specific hazard register and traceability from hazard → control → test → residual risk → post-market signal** | SOP-PENG-001 has a risk register and threat model outputs, but it does not require an AI hazard/risk register that traces each AI hazard to risk controls, validation tests, acceptance criteria, residual-risk decision, deployer information, and post-market monitoring indicators. | Article 9(2), 9(5), 9(6), and 9(8) collectively require lifecycle risk identification, targeted controls, acceptable residual risk, and testing against defined metrics and thresholds. |
| **18. Integration with post-market monitoring plan for continuous compliance** | The SOP’s post-deployment phase does not require a post-market monitoring plan for high-risk AI systems or continuous evaluation of compliance with Chapter III, Section 2 requirements. | Article 72(2)-(3) requires active and systematic collection, documentation, and analysis of relevant performance data throughout the lifetime of the system, based on a post-market monitoring plan. Article 9(2)(c) requires those data to feed back into risk evaluation. |

## Bottom line

SOP-PENG-001 is a **partial foundation** because it contains lifecycle controls, security requirements, threat modeling, residual-risk documentation, testing gates, release controls, and post-deployment vulnerability monitoring. However, for **high-risk AI systems**, it is missing the AI Act Article 9-specific risk management elements: health/safety/fundamental-rights hazard analysis, intended-use and foreseeable-misuse evaluation, AI-specific testing metrics and probabilistic thresholds, vulnerable-group analysis, deployer-context analysis, Article 13 deployer instructions/training, and a post-market AI monitoring feedback loop.

Compliance level: partial

(66) 'general-purpose AI system' means an AI system which is based on a general-purpose AI model and which has the capability to serve a variety of purposes, both for direct use as well as for integration in other AI systems.

(67) 'floating-point operation' means any mathematical operation or assignment involving floating-point numbers, which are a subset of the real numbers typically represented on computers by an integer of fixed precision scaled by an integer exponent of a fixed base.

(68) 'downstream provider' means a provider of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, which integrates an AI model, regardless of whether the AI model is provided by themselves and vertically integrated or provided by another entity based on contractual relations.

## Article 4: AI Literacy

Providers and deployers of AI systems shall take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf, taking into account their technical knowledge, experience, education and training and the context the AI systems are to be used in, and considering the persons or groups of persons on whom the AI systems are to be used.

**Article 9: Risk Management System**
### Article 9: Risk Management System

1. A risk management system shall be established, implemented, documented and maintained in relation to high-risk AI systems.

2. The risk management system shall be understood as a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of a high-risk AI system, requiring regular systematic review and updating. It shall comprise the following steps:

(a) the identification and analysis of the known and the reasonably foreseeable risks that the high-risk AI system can pose to health, safety or fundamental rights when the high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose;

(b) the estimation and evaluation of the risks that may emerge when the high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose, and under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse;

(c) the evaluation of other risks possibly arising, based on the analysis of data gathered from the post-market monitoring system referred to in Article 72;

(d) the adoption of appropriate and targeted risk management measures designed to address the risks identified pursuant to point (a).

3. The risks referred to in this Article shall concern only those which may be reasonably mitigated or eliminated through the development or design of the high-risk AI system, or the provision of adequate technical information.

4. The risk management measures referred to in paragraph 2, point (d), shall give due consideration to the effects and possible interaction resulting from the combined application of the requirements set out in this Section, with a view to minimising risks more effectively while achieving an appropriate balance in implementing the measures to fulfil those requirements.

5. The risk management measures referred to in paragraph 2, point (d), shall be such that the relevant residual risk associated with each hazard, as well as the overall residual risk of the high-risk AI systems is judged to be acceptable. In identifying the most appropriate risk management measures, the following shall be ensured:

(a) elimination or reduction of risks identified and evaluated pursuant to paragraph 2 in as far as technically feasible through adequate design and development of the high-risk AI system;

(b) where appropriate, implementation of adequate mitigation and control measures addressing risks that cannot be eliminated;

(c) provision of information required pursuant to Article 13 and, where appropriate, training to deployers.

**Article 17: Quality Management System**
### Article 17: Quality Management System

1. Providers of high-risk AI systems shall put a quality management system in place that ensures compliance with this Regulation. That system shall be documented in a systematic and orderly manner in the form of written policies, procedures and instructions, and shall include at least the following aspects:

(a) a strategy for regulatory compliance, including compliance with conformity assessment procedures and procedures for the management of modifications to the high-risk AI system;

(b) techniques, procedures and systematic actions to be used for the design, design control and design verification of the high-risk AI system;

(c) techniques, procedures and systematic actions to be used for the development, quality control and quality assurance of the high-risk AI system;

(d) examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after the development of the high-risk AI system, and the frequency with which they have to be carried out;

(e) technical specifications, including standards, to be applied and, where the relevant harmonised standards are not applied in full or do not cover all of the relevant requirements set out in Section 2, the means to be used to ensure that the high-risk AI system complies with those requirements;

(f) systems and procedures for data management, including data acquisition, data collection, data analysis, data labelling, data storage, data filtration, data mining, data aggregation, data retention and any other operation regarding the data that is performed before and for the purpose of the placing on the market or the putting into service of high-risk AI systems;

(g) the risk management system referred to in Article 9;

(h) the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system, in accordance with Article 72;

(i) procedures related to the reporting of a serious incident in accordance with Article 73;

(j) the handling of communication with national competent authorities, other relevant authorities, including those providing or supporting the access to data, notified bodies, other operators, customers or other interested parties;

(k) systems and procedures for record-keeping of all relevant documentation and information;

(l) resource management, including security-of-supply related measures;

(m) an accountability framework setting out the responsibilities of the management and other staff with regard to all the aspects listed in this paragraph.

### Article 27: Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment for High-Risk AI Systems

1. Prior to deploying a high-risk AI system referred to in Article 6(2), with the exception of high-risk AI systems intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III, deployers that are bodies governed by public law, or are private entities providing public services, and deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in points 5 (b) and (c) of Annex III, shall perform an assessment of the impact on fundamental rights that the use of such system may produce. (b) a description of the period of time within which, and the frequency with which, each high-risk AI system is intended to be used;

(d) the specific risks of harm likely to have an impact on the categories of natural persons or groups of persons identified pursuant to point (c) of this paragraph, taking into account the information given by the provider pursuant to Article 13;

(e) a description of the implementation of human oversight measures, according to the instructions for use;

2. The obligation laid down in paragraph 1 applies to the first use of the high-risk AI system. ### Article 13: Transparency and Provision of Information to Deployers

1. High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way as to ensure that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system's output and use it appropriately. An appropriate type and degree of transparency shall be ensured with a view to achieving compliance with the relevant obligations of the provider and deployer set out in Section 3.

2. High-risk AI systems shall be accompanied by instructions for use in an appropriate digital format or otherwise that include concise, complete, correct and clear information that is relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers.

3. The instructions for use shall contain at least the following information:

(a) the identity and the contact details of the provider and, where applicable, of its authorised representative;

(b) the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance of the high-risk AI system, including:

(i) its intended purpose;

(ii) the level of accuracy, including its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity referred to in Article 15 against which the high-risk AI system has been tested and validated and which can be expected, and any known and foreseeable circumstances that may have an impact on that expected level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity;

(iii) any known or foreseeable circumstance, related to the use of the high-risk AI system in accordance with its intended purpose or under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse, which may lead to risks to the health and safety or fundamental rights referred to in Article 9(2);

(iv) where applicable, the technical capabilities and characteristics of the high-risk AI system to provide information that is relevant to explain its output;

(v) when appropriate, its performance regarding specific persons or groups of persons on which the system is intended to be used;

(vi) when appropriate, specifications for the input data, or any other relevant information in terms of the training, validation and testing data sets used, taking into account the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system;

(vii) where applicable, information to enable deployers to interpret the output of the high-risk AI system and use it appropriately;

(c) the changes to the high-risk AI system and its performance which have been predetermined by the provider at the moment of the initial conformity assessment, if any;

(d) the human oversight measures referred to in Article 14, including the technical measures put in place to facilitate the interpretation of the outputs of the high-risk AI systems by the deployers;

**Article 72: Post-Market Monitoring by Providers and Post-Market Monitoring Plan for High-Risk AI Systems**
### Article 72: Post-Market Monitoring by Providers and Post-Market Monitoring Plan for High-Risk AI Systems

1. Providers shall establish and document a post-market monitoring system in a manner that is proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high-risk AI system.

2. The post-market monitoring system shall actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant data which may be provided by deployers or which may be collected through other sources on the performance of high-risk AI systems throughout their lifetime, and which allow the provider to evaluate the continuous compliance of AI systems with the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2. Where relevant, post-market monitoring shall include an analysis of the interaction with other AI systems. This obligation shall not cover sensitive operational data of deployers which are law enforcement authorities.

3. The post-market monitoring system shall be based on a post-market monitoring plan. The post-market monitoring plan shall be part of the technical documentation referred to in Annex IV. The Commission shall adopt an implementing act laying down detailed provisions establishing a template for the post-market monitoring plan and the list of elements to be included in the plan by 2 February 2026. That implementing act shall be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Article 98(2).

4. For high-risk AI systems covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, where a post-market monitoring system and plan are already established under that legislation, in order to ensure consistency, avoid duplications and minimise additional burdens, providers shall have a choice of integrating, as appropriate, the necessary elements described in paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 using the template referred in paragraph 3 into systems and plans already existing under that legislation, provided that it achieves an equivalent level of protection.

The first subparagraph of this paragraph shall also apply to high-risk AI systems referred to in point 5 of Annex III placed on the market or put into service by financial institutions that are subject to requirements under Union financial services law regarding their internal governance, arrangements or processes.

# Chapter I: General Provisions (Articles 1-4)

## Article 1: Subject Matter

1. The purpose of this Regulation is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI), while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union and supporting innovation.

2. This Regulation lays down:

(a) harmonised rules for the placing on the market, the putting into service, and the use of AI systems in the Union;

(b) prohibitions of certain AI practices;

(c) specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems;

(d) harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems;

(e) harmonised rules for the placing on the market of general-purpose AI models;

(f) rules on market monitoring, market surveillance, governance and enforcement;

(g) measures to support innovation, with a particular focus on SMEs, including startups.

## Article 2: Scope

1. This Regulation applies to:

(a) providers placing on the market or putting into service AI systems or placing on the market general-purpose AI models in the Union, irrespective of whether those providers are established or located within the Union or in a third country;

(b) deployers of AI systems that have their place of establishment or are located within the Union;

(c) providers and deployers of AI systems that have their place of establishment or are located in a third country, where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union;

(d) importers and distributors of AI systems;

(e) product manufacturers placing on the market or putting into service an AI system together with their product and under their own name or trademark;

(f) authorised representatives of providers, which are not established in the Union;

(g) affected persons that are located in the Union.

**Article 12: Record-Keeping**
### Article 12: Record-Keeping

1. High-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system.

2. In order to ensure a level of traceability of the functioning of a high-risk AI system that is appropriate to the intended purpose of the system, logging capabilities shall enable the recording of events relevant for:

(a) identifying situations that may result in the high-risk AI system presenting a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) or in a substantial modification;

(b) facilitating the post-market monitoring referred to in Article 72; and

(c) monitoring the operation of high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 26(5).

3. For high-risk AI systems referred to in point 1 (a), of Annex III, the logging capabilities shall provide, at a minimum:

(a) recording of the period of each use of the system (start date and time and end date and time of each use);

(b) the reference database against which input data has been checked by the system;

(c) the input data for which the search has led to a match;

(d) the identification of the natural persons involved in the verification of the results, as referred to in Article 14(5).
